judges.label: judge:evidence

scores.strongest_point: It has the closest published analogues. LRT (frozen Qwen3-8B, a ~11M recurrent refiner writing soft tokens) gains more with each cycle and beats a non-recurrent refiner of the same budget, 56.7 vs 47.5 on Countdown [shown, R4]. INTACT shows that progressive re-encoding by the frozen LM wins, 84.4 vs 82.0 [shown]. It also avoids the failure this repo measured: no backbone layer ever receives its own output. Loop-1L B did, and its start loss was 2.56 vs 0.72 and it collapsed to 29.6 at 12 passes [shown, repo]. Slots committed to the cache are read natively by every layer, DeltaNet/conv included, at about zero per-token decode cost [suggested].
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: Two problems. (1) Budget: an 11.6M randomly initialised refiner gets 418 steps x 16 = 6,688 examples, about 8% of one pass over the 86k training rows [shown, counted]. LRT trained 30 epochs per task, and Newt concluded 'budget, not architecture' [shown, R1]. (2) It has no control trained at L=1 only. Under random-L training the lap-1 floor is degraded (McLeish [shown]), so a gain from lap 1 to lap 8 overstates what the loop does. The refiner can also cross-attend to the context directly, so it could do all its work in lap 1. Separately, the TTFT estimate is optimistic by about 1.5-2x (see errors).
factual_errors: The TTFT reasoning is wrong in two places. '16/420 = 38 ms from measured prefill' applies long-prompt prefill throughput to a 16-token pass, and that pass is limited by memory bandwidth. '170 GB/s' is about 2x the measured effective decode bandwidth (~70-78 GB/s: ~1.3-1.4 GB per token in 18 ms). A realistic lap is ~80-120 ms, so L=8 (9 passes) is ~0.8-1.1 s for 1 agent and ~1.2-1.7 s for 2 [suggested]. The other agent's time-averaged rate then falls toward ~30-31 tok/s, not 32-33 [suggested].
Overhead '~7% at L=8': village prompts are p50 1,143 / p90 1,674 tokens without the few-shot prefix [shown, tokenized today]. 144 slot tokens is 7-13% depending on the prefix. Minor.
The other numbers I checked are correct: LoRA count 10.8M, refiner 11.6M, expert union 0.64, INTACT, CODI, HybridAgent and Coda-Forno figures [shown].

scores.strongest_point: The cleanest of the cheap designs. It is exactly arm A at step 0 (Wo zero-init). Each lap costs about 245 MB of reads (~4-6 ms), so TTFT is about +45 ms and decode about +3% [suggested, arithmetic checked]. It has the strongest anti-decoration package: a control trained at L=1, a detached hinge on L+4, swap and zero-board lesions, and a pre-fixed halting rule based on oracle headroom. That rule follows R3's evidence that halts buy compute, not accuracy.
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: Each lap feeds layer 11 (LFM 18) its own output. That is the self-fed re-run pattern that failed here (Loop-1L B [shown]) and in Newt (<=5% of the signal went through recurrence [shown, R1]). It is damped, but there is no norm clamp, and LOOM reports hidden-variance growth in looped MoE layers [shown]. Each lap also reads only ONE layer's KV. DCA's coprocessor scored 23.2 reading the last layer vs 26.8 reading the full KV [shown], so the reads are weak. In effect this is the starting recipe without the halt, so it barely meets the brief's demand to beat that prior.
factual_errors: Cites 'zero-init gates beat random init (Flamingo 70.7 vs 66.5)'. In R4, Flamingo's 70.7 vs 66.5 is gate vs no gate. The zero-init vs random-init result is LLaMA-Adapter, 83.85 vs 40.77 [shown, R4].
The expert-union formula is written as 64*(1-(63/64)^64). The correct form for 16 slots x top-4 is 64*(1-(60/64)^16) = 41.2. The value (~40.7) is nearly the same, so harmless.
Correct: the every-token arithmetic (29.5 tok/s), 3,426 validation rows at depth >=3, block LoRA 401,408, sites 3.15M / 10.5M [shown, checked].

scores.strongest_point: It is exactly arm A at init (per-head tanh(alpha) = 0) and adds only 0.14M new parameters. Every lap is a full-depth re-read of the context by the frozen backbone (+ LoRA) over token-like inputs, so no layer is fed its own output. Training costs only +4-6% compute and fits wherever arm A fits. Decode cost is ~0.01%. The code facts are accurate: the GDN/short-conv paths continue from the cache, and the in-place copy_ needs an assigning cache subclass [shown, checked in transformers 5.20.2].
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: The feedback path is tiny: a rank-64 linear map of the final-normed slot state, fed back into embeddings (Coconut-style). The evidence says this is weak. Raw or identity hidden-state feedback scored 71.4 vs 88.2 (HybridAgent [shown]), and LRT's gains grew with refiner size (7->28M [shown]). The board is read only at the 6 (Qwen) or 10 (LFM) attention layers through a parallel branch, and is never committed to the sequence, so the DeltaNet/conv layers never see it. A fixed point by lap 2-3 is likely, and there is no control trained at L=1.
factual_errors: Per-lap Mac cost assumes 100-150 GB/s for batched reads, against a measured effective ~70-78 GB/s in decode. A lap is more likely ~60-80 ms than 25-55 ms, so TTFT is ~0.5-0.9 s at 8 laps with 2 agents [suggested]. Minor.

'Arm B adds depth but not a query that changes between rounds' overstates the difference: B's hidden states, and so its queries, do change between passes. The real difference is that B re-runs every position [suggested].
Correct: param counts 139,312 / 278,848, LoRA 10,822,656 (matches my per-layer count), 1,558 validation rows at depth 4-6, layer indices [shown].

scores.strongest_point: Best controls of any design: a C1 arm trained at R=1 only (same parameters and positions), swap and mean-board lesions, per-lap delta-norm, and a detached hinge that cannot reward a weak lap 1. Pass and fail marks are fixed in advance. The board lives in the sequence, so later tokens and later turns read it natively. Decode cost is ~0.5% and the burst ~0.15-0.4 s [suggested]. The param counts check out: 1.80M Qwen, 1.65M LFM.
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: The laps re-run the pretrained band (8-11 / 16-23, all MoE at LFM) on its own output. That is the operation that broke Loop-1L B (start loss 2.56 vs 0.72, collapse at 12 [shown, repo]), here confined to 16 slots. There is no zero-init gate on the board read, so at init with R>1 the answer already attends to off-distribution slot states. The design says the opposite.
factual_errors: 'The board comes out of real layers via a zero-init LoRA, so it stays near normal hidden states' is wrong at R>1. A zero-init LoRA means the band is the pretrained band, and re-applying it to its own output is what produced off-distribution states in Loop-1L B [shown]. Damping and the norm hold mitigate this but do not prevent it.
'The Loop-1L failure cannot hit text' is overstated. Text never enters the loop but attends to the looped slots through ungated native attention [suggested].
The burst uses 150 GB/s, about 2x the effective decode bandwidth, so the true burst is likely ~2x the stated 145 ms (still small) [suggested].
Correct: 20 KB per board position, 39.5% of validation at depth >=3, the INTACT swap cost of 7.9, and 4M tokens in 13 h at 4x21 tok/s [shown, checked].

scores.strongest_point: It is the easiest design to inspect. Every lap is decodable through the frozen LM head, so per-lap draft accuracy and wrong->right / right->wrong flips are direct measurements (R3 lesson 10). The answer-length statistics are correct: p50 3 / p90 13 / p99 25 tokens including EOS [shown, re-tokenized today]. The corruption curriculum targets the main tau-bench failure class (wrong IDs and arguments) [suggested].
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: The Jacobi part converges to the greedy autoregressive answer of the same model. A rising per-lap draft curve is therefore partly mechanical: Jacobi needs about as many laps as the answer has tokens, and village answers are ~3 tokens. The final AR decode can simply copy that draft, so the laps risk recomputing what plain decoding would produce. Only the verifier and refiner add new computation. It is the most complex design: three losses, 248k-vocab logits on every lap (~2 GB), 8.7M / 34.8M new parameters on 418 steps, and the largest TTFT (~1-1.8 s per turn, plus re-prefill after rollback).
factual_errors: 'Jacobi iteration has a fixed point, so laps past convergence leave the draft unchanged' does not hold once a learned refiner rewrites b every lap. The combined map has no guaranteed fixed point, and Jacobi's own fixed point is the plain greedy answer [suggested].
'Village SE about 0.5 points' is the binomial SE. The noise that matters is the seed spread (arm A 66.06-67.78, SD ~0.9) [shown, brief], so a 3-seed mean difference has SE ~0.8.
Active parameters are given as 2.53B. R4 / the model card say 2.45B. Minor.
Correct: M_tool SE ~2.7 on 322 turns, the expert union of 55.9 at 32 tokens [shown, checked].

scores.strongest_point: An honest prior: it admits that no paper shows lap-specialised experts helping a frozen backbone. It has a decisive D-fixed control (M=1), and its kill rules are stated in advance. The LFM pre-check (expert Jaccard overlap across laps, no training) is cheap and useful. TTFT is the lowest of all designs (~30-40 ms) [suggested].
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: The evidence runs against routing. Untied routers moved loss by under 0.01 nats, and trained routers re-pick the same experts (Tying the Loop, SMELT [shown, R3]). It uses Gumbel/straight-through Switch routing over four frozen layers, and each layer's LoRA and thought expert trains on only ~1/4 of the slot-laps in 418 steps. It also feeds a layer-16 residual state (z = h[T-2] after layer 15) into pool layers 3/7/11, which are pretrained on much shallower residual statistics. That depth mismatch is not acknowledged.
factual_errors: The per-lap read undercounts. Slots routed to 4 different pool layers touch ~4 x 64(1-(60/64)^4) ~ 58 experts and four layers' attention weights (~24 MB), not 41 experts and 5.9 MB, so ~330 MB and ~4.5 ms per lap. Immaterial for speed.
Correct: param counts 8.10M / 21.9M, the LFM router code (sigmoid; expert_bias affects selection only), the DCA 26.8 vs 23.2 KV read [shown, checked].

ideas_worth_grafting: From D2/D5: add a C1 arm (same parameters as STS, trained and tested only at L=1). Under random-L training the lap-1 floor is degraded (McLeish [shown]). Without C1, lap8 - lap1 cannot tell loop work from extra parameters. Pass mark: STS@8 - C1 >= 2.

From D2/D5: add the detached monotone hinge 0.1-0.5 * relu(CE(L') - sg(CE(L))) with L' > L. It pushes later laps to be no worse and cannot reward a weak lap 1 [untested]. Answers are ~3 tokens, so a per-lap answer CE is cheap.

From D1: a per-head zero-init tanh(alpha) gate on answer->slot attention, so step 0 is exactly arm A rather than 'A + 16 pause tokens'. DCA saw pause tokens make first-token perplexity worse (11.63 vs 10.96 [shown]).

From D1: run FSB (feedback without a refiner) as an ablation arm of STS. It is the cheapest test of whether the 11.6M refiner earns its place. Also reuse D1's cache-fork recipe: an assigning cache subclass for training, and a clone of the GDN state plus crop for inference.

From D4: decode every lap's slots through the frozen LM head. Log per-lap draft exact-match and wrong->right / right->wrong flips on 1k dev rows (R3 lesson 10). Run D4's step-0 check: an untrained board must add <= 0.10 nats of answer CE.

From D6's own risk 3 and D4: a budget arm (418 vs 1,254 steps, with A also at 1,254). STS trains an 11.6M module on ~8% of one pass over the training data, so it is the design most exposed to 'budget, not architecture'.
From D5: the halting rule, fixed now. If held-out oracle headroom (best L per row minus best fixed L) is < 2 points, never add a halt. Otherwise use only a post-hoc KL exit fit on dev.

From D3/D5 (LFM only, no training): time an 8-lap 16-slot burst on the Mac with 2 agents, and log lap-to-lap expert Jaccard overlap, before any rental. Use the measured TTFT instead of the 38-52 ms/lap estimate. If the burst is too slow, K=8 is the fallback.
From D2 (LFM only): a zero-init cross-turn carry z0 += tanh(g) * z_prev. It is motivated by Nemotron-Cascade 2's +3-5 from keeping the latest-turn reasoning [suggested].

For all designs: choose the lap count on dev. Dev has max depth 3 (counted today: 305/1552/1331/812 rows at depths 0-3). The depth 4-6 slice (1,558 rows) exists only in validation, so it must not be used for tuning.
judges.rationale:
Ranking: D6 (Silent Think Slots), then D5, D1, D2, D4, D3. All six designs pass the speed gate, because each thinks in one burst per turn rather than at every token. The gap between them comes from evidence and from how hard it is to tell real lap work from decoration.

**Village pilot (Qwen3.5-0.8B; stage-1 village data, not v1)**
- What the repo has measured [shown]: re-running the middle layers at every position (arm B) gave +0.40 over A, inside the ~1.2-point seed spread. The 1-pass lesion cost -7.7 but bought no generalisation. Depth is A's weakest axis (-8).
- The PASS bar (+3 over both A and B) is about 4 standard errors of a 3-seed mean difference. Every designer predicts +1.8 to +3.0 and gives 25-40% odds of passing. I think that is fair to slightly optimistic given 418 steps [suggested].
- Two structural risks apply to every design:
  - Training uses ~8% of one pass over the training data [shown, counted]. Large new modules (D6, D4) suffer most.
  - Training with random lap counts degrades the lap-1 floor (McLeish [shown]). Only D2 and D5 include the control trained at 1 lap that separates loop work from extra parameters.

**Why D6 is first**
- It transplants the two strongest frozen-backbone results: LRT's recurrent refiner over soft tokens (more cycles help; a non-recurrent refiner of the same budget scored 47.5 vs 56.7 [shown]) and INTACT's progressive re-encoding (84.4 vs 82.0 [shown]).
- It avoids the operation that failed in this repo: Loop-1L B fed layers their own output and its start loss rose from 0.72 to 2.56 [shown].
- Its weaknesses can be fixed by grafting (the 1-lap control, the hinge, a zero-init gate). Its real risk is training budget, which is an empirical question D6 already tests.

**The rest**
- **D5** is cheap, safe at init and has the best halting discipline. But it is essentially the starting recipe: a self-fed single layer reading one layer's KV. R1's retrofit evidence (Newt) and DCA's weaker shallow read count against it.
- **D1** is D6's minimal ablation. It is the most trainable design, but its rank-64 hidden-state feedback is the variant the literature finds weakest.
- **D2** has excellent controls but loops the band on its own output with an ungated board read.
- **D4** is the most measurable, but its Jacobi laps largely recompute the greedy answer at the highest cost in complexity and TTFT.
- **D3**'s routing has evidence against it (Tying the Loop, SMELT), and it feeds deep-layer states into shallow layers.

**LFM2.5 / tau2 (kept separate)**
- No latent method has been evaluated on multi-turn tool use [shown, R2/R4]. The 23->30 gap is p~0.10 on n=40 [shown].
- Expected tau2 gains for every design are therefore untested and likely inside noise unless all retail tasks and repeated trials are used.
- D6's Mac TTFT has to be measured: my estimate is ~1.2-1.7 s per turn with 2 agents, against its own ~0.7 s. Decode stays at ~35 tok/s [suggested].

**Summary for Ben**
All six ideas let the big model "think" once before it answers instead of at every word, so they all keep the Mac fast enough. The winner, D6, follows the published recipe with the best track record: a small helper nudges 16 hidden "thinking slots", and the frozen model re-reads them. It also avoids the trick that broke our own Loop-1L test. Its biggest risk is that our short practice run gives the helper too little training. To check whether the extra laps really help, compare against a copy trained with just one lap.

judges.label: judge:systems

scores.strongest_point: Has the best evidence of any design that the mechanism works on a frozen backbone (shown in R2/R4: LRT's recurrent refiner beat a non-recurrent refiner of equal budget, 56.7 vs 47.5; INTACT's progressive re-encoding beat joint construction, 84.4 vs 82.0). Each lap is a full 24/40-layer re-read whose queries carry the last lap's findings. The slots sit in the sequence, so every attention layer and every GDN/conv layer reads them natively, and per-token decode is untouched. The controls are the right ones: P = pause-only, A32 = parameter-matched, S = swap, F = frozen.
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: The Mac burst cost is underestimated by about 2x (suggested). One 16-slot lap reads about 8.9 GB of weights, about 41 of 64 experts in each of 38 layers. At the ~76 GB/s effective bandwidth seen in decode, that is ~115 ms per lap, so L=8 is ~1.0 s alone and ~1.5 s with 2 agents, not the claimed 0.45-0.7 s. There is also no arm trained with the same refiner at L=1 only, and step 0 is 'A + 16 pause tokens', not arm A.
factual_errors: 'Measured prefill gives 16/420 = 38 ms per lap' misapplies long-prompt prefill throughput, where expert reads are shared across hundreds of tokens, to a 16-token chunk, which is bandwidth-bound. The likely cost is ~115 ms per lap (suggested, arithmetic from the config: 41.2 experts x 38 layers x 5.3 MB + ~0.4 GB dense).
Its 170 GB/s is close to the M1 Pro's 200 GB/s peak. Decode on Ben's Mac effectively runs at ~70-76 GB/s (2.45B active params x 0.5625 B / 18 ms) (suggested).
'At init exactly A + 16 pause tokens' is correct, but that is not arm A. R4 (shown) records that pause tokens worsened first-token perplexity in Liu et al. (11.63 vs 10.96).

Checked and correct: the parameter counts (11.6M pilot, 29.1M LFM), the arm-A LoRA count of 10.82M, the in-place copy_ in LinearAttentionLayer, and that ShortConv keeps only conv state (all shown, read in transformers 5.20.2).

scores.strongest_point: Cheapest and cleanest to implement. Step 0 is exactly arm A because the site Wo is zero-init. Each lap is one attention+MLP layer reading a KV cache that already exists, so no GDN or conv state is touched and no cache shim is needed. On LFM a lap is ~245 MB, about 3-4 ms, so +26-45 ms TTFT; decode is ~34 tok/s per agent with 2 agents. The speed arithmetic checks out. It has the best halting logic: an oracle-headroom rule fixed in advance, plus an arm trained at L=1 only to separate laps from parameters.
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: Expected gain is limited. Every lap reads one depth's KV (Qwen layer 11 / LFM layer 18). The board reaches the answer only through rank-256, 4-head cross-attention at 3 Qwen sites, and Flamingo-style evidence says sparse read sites lose capacity (shown in R4: a single middle site scored 59.8 vs 70.7 with a site at every layer). One frozen layer applied repeatedly is also the setting most likely to hit a fixed point by lap 2-3 (shown for v1 only).
factual_errors: Expert union uses 64*(1-(63/64)^64)=40.6 rather than 64*(1-(60/64)^16)=41.2. The difference is negligible.
The 1.54 contention factor applied to small-kernel overhead is a heuristic, not a measurement. It is labelled untested, which is acceptable.
Checked and correct: 1000/(28.2+8*28.2/40)=29.5 tok/s; the parameter counts 3.56M / 10.7M and the 18.35M frozen copy of layer 11; 3,426 validation rows at depth >=3 (shown, counted).

scores.strongest_point: The smallest design (0.14M new parameters at 0.8B) with an exact arm-A start (tanh(alpha)=0). The board read reuses the frozen q/k/v, so decode costs about 164 KB per token, effectively zero. Each lap is a full-depth re-read of the prompt from a forked cache. It correctly found the in-place copy_ problem in HF linear-attention caches and the multi-token GDN/ShortConv continuation path, and both check out in transformers 5.20.2.
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: The refiner is only a rank-64 linear map from the final hidden state back to the input embedding, which is close to Coconut-style feedback. With answer-only loss, Coconut without a curriculum stayed at the no-CoT level (shown, R2). All lap parameters get zero gradient until alpha moves, so the 'board ignored' failure seen in Newt is the likely outcome. There is no arm trained with the same parameters at N=1, so decoration is only half measurable. The slot RoPE positions overlap the answer's and are unmasked.
factual_errors: 'Non-expert ~0.75B, 1.24 GB per token' is too low. From the config, non-expert active parameters including the tied 128k x 2048 head come to ~1.0B, giving ~2.45B active and ~1.38 GB per token at 4.5 bits (suggested, arithmetic).
'+6% compute (64/1000)' assumes ~1k-token prompts. Village prompts are ~2k, so the overhead is ~3%. The error is conservative.
The 25-55 ms per lap assumes 100-150 GB/s. At ~76 GB/s an 8-slot lap (~5.6 GB) takes ~75 ms, so 8 laps take ~0.6 s with one agent (suggested).

Design slip, not arithmetic: slots occupy positions T-1..T+K-2, the same RoPE positions as the last prompt token and the first answer tokens, and answer queries attend them with no mask (shown from the pseudocode; effect untested).
Checked and correct: 139,312 and 278,848 parameters, the 10,822,656 LoRA count, 1,558 rows at depth 4-6, 25.8 experts for 8 slots.

scores.strongest_point: Keeps text out of the loop entirely, so the Loop-1L failure (start loss 2.56 vs 0.72 when all positions re-ran the MoE band; shown) cannot reach text tokens. It also has the best decoration controls: a C1 arm with the same parameters trained at R=1, a detached 'later laps must not be worse' hinge, swap and mean-board tests, and a lap-to-lap change ratio. Boards stay in the cache across turns. The decode cost (20 KB per board position, ~0.5%) checks out.
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: Step 0 is not arm A. The 16 slots are in the sequence with no zero gate, and the damped update (alpha 0.5) plus the norm hold to rms(Z0) means even R=1 produces a hidden state the upper stack has never seen. It also still re-runs frozen MoE layers 16-23 with a frozen router on their own outputs (over slots only), the setting where LOOM reports expert-selection collapse (shown, from-scratch models). The cache snapshot/restore over a band, plus a per-lap upper-stack fork for the per-lap CE, is the most implementation work after D4.
factual_errors: 'The board comes out of real layers via a zero-init LoRA, so it stays near normal hidden states' is not true at init. z = 0.5*Z0 + 0.5*band(Z0), rescaled to rms(Z0), is not the band's natural output, and the residual norm at layer b is forced back to the layer-a norm (shown from the pseudocode).
Burst arithmetic uses 150 GB/s. At ~76 GB/s, R=8 is ~0.28 s with one agent (9 GB first pass plus 7 x 1.75 GB band laps), still small (suggested).
Checked and correct: 20 KB per board position, 41 experts for 16 tokens, think-LoRA counts 1.80M / 1.61M, 39.5% of validation at depth >=3.

scores.strongest_point: Has the richest per-lap signal. The frozen LM head decodes a draft every lap, which gives a per-lap readout and flip counts for free. Free confidence checks and a learned verifier set the step size. The corruption curriculum, which swaps one entity in the draft, directly trains repair of the most common tau-bench error (wrong ID or argument; shown in R4).
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: The Jacobi shift confounds the main decoration test. Draft slot j is fed lap k-1's token j-1, and the fixed point of Jacobi iteration is the frozen model's own greedy answer. Per-lap draft accuracy and wrong-to-right flips therefore rise by construction, even when no reasoning is added. It is also the most expensive on the Mac (a 32-slot full pass is ~11.9 GB per lap, so ~1.25 s at N=8 with one agent and ~2 s with two). It is the most complex to train: three losses, 248k-vocab logits every lap, a refiner and a verifier.
factual_errors: TTFT of 0.8-1.2 s assumes 80-120 GB/s. At ~76 GB/s it is ~1.25 s with one agent and ~1.8-2.5 s with two, so the '~32 tok/s time-averaged' figure is optimistic. It still passes on per-token decode, and K=16 / N=4 is a cheap fix (suggested).

Failure test 1 ('draft exact-match at lap 8 minus lap 1') cannot detect decoration, because Jacobi convergence produces that rise with no reasoning gain (suggested, from the mechanism). The decisive test should be accuracy of the final autoregressive answer against arm A's greedy answer, by lap.
Step 0 is not arm A. The 24 board positions are in the sequence with no gate. Its own test 3 checks this, which is good.
Checked and correct: 55.9 experts for 32 tokens, 11.9 GB per lap, 8.73M / 34.8M parameters, village SE ~0.5 points.

scores.strongest_point: Cheap on the Mac (one layer per slot per lap, ~3-4 ms per lap, ~35 tok/s decode) and frank about its weak prior. The D-fixed control (M=1) and the route histograms make it clear whether routing is decoration. The zero-training Mac check of expert overlap between laps is worth doing whatever design wins.
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: No evidence supports lap-routed experts on a frozen backbone (shown, R3 section 8). In 'Tying the Loop', untying the routers moved loss by under 0.01 nats (shown). Gumbel top-1 straight-through routing over 4 frozen layers is fragile in 418 steps. The board starts from the layer-15 residual and is fed into layer 3's attention, a depth mismatch. Even if the board works, routing is likely to be the decoration.
factual_errors: The per-lap MoE read assumes all 16 slots reach one pool layer (41 experts, 218 MB). The load-balance loss spreads them over 4 layers, about 4 slots each, giving ~14 experts x 4 layers, about 58 experts (~0.3 GB, ~4 ms per lap). Small, but the direction is wrong (suggested).

Checked and correct: in Lfm2MoeTopKRouter, sigmoid weights are used for both selection and weighting, and expert_bias affects selection only (shown, code); the PeekCache hook works because both attention classes call past_key_values.update (shown); the 8.10M / 21.9M parameter tables are right.

ideas_worth_grafting: From D1, an exact arm-A start: put the answer-to-slot attention on a per-layer zero-init tanh(alpha) gate, either as D1's parallel slot-KV branch or as a gated slot-key logit bias. Step 0 then equals arm A rather than A plus pause tokens, and the gate is a logged 'share of signal through the board' meter, the decisive metric from Newt.
From D2/D5, a control arm trained at L=1 only with the same parameters and positions (D2's C1, D5's D1). This separates laps from extra parameters. D6's P (0 laps) and A32 do not do that.

From D2/D5, the detached hinge relu(CE(L+k) - sg(CE(L))) on a fraction of rows, so later laps cannot get worse, and laps up to 12 inside training (D5: L 9-12 with probability 0.1, no gradient on the early laps), so 12 does not collapse the way Loop-1L B did (40.7 -> 29.6, shown).

From D5, a halting rule fixed in advance: add a halt only if held-out oracle headroom (best L per row minus best fixed L) is >= 2 points, and then only as a post-hoc KL or confidence exit, never a jointly trained gate (shown in R3 that joint gates entangle with the trajectory they read).
From D5, think only at decision points on LFM: after each user message or tool result, and right after <|tool_call_start|> when text came first. Run no trigger on uncertain tokens.

From D4, a free per-lap readout as a diagnostic, not a loss: decode the slot hidden states through the frozen LM head each lap, and count per-lap wrong-to-right and right-to-wrong flips of the final answer on held-out rows (TaH-style overthinking curve). Optionally feed entropy and margin to the refiner as zero-parameter inputs.

From D3/D5, zero-training Mac checks before any LFM spend: (a) time an L=8 burst with 16 and with 8 slots at 12k context with 2 agents running, using real mlx-lm, not the 16/420 prefill extrapolation; (b) measure Jaccard overlap of the experts each slot selects across laps; if above 0.8, add a per-lap router bias.
Cost knob from D1/D6: K=8 slots cuts the expert union per layer from ~41 to ~26 of 64, about 37% less burst per lap on LFM. Pre-register K=8 vs K=16 as the one speed ablation.
From D2/D5, a zero-init cross-turn carry (z0 += tanh(g)*z_prev) is reasonable at LFM scale only. Keep it out of the village pilot so the pilot tests one change.
From D4, the corruption curriculum (swap one ID or argument in a draft and train repair) as a later LFM-only ablation targeting wrong-argument failures. Do not add it to the pilot.
judges.rationale:
Judged as a systems and training engineer. Labels: shown = read in code or config, or measured. Suggested = my arithmetic or an inference. Untested = nobody has run it.

**Speed.** Every design passes the per-token gate, because none runs laps during decode (suggested). D1, D2 and D6 add only 8-16 positions to the attention reads. D3 and D5 add about 10 MB of low-rank cross-attention per token, giving about 34-35 tok/s per agent with 2 agents.

The real differences are in the per-turn burst. I recomputed it from the LFM2.5 config (suggested):
- Effective decode bandwidth: 2.45B active params x ~0.5625 B / 18 ms ≈ 76 GB/s.
- One 4-bit expert ≈ 5.3 MB.
- Expected experts touched per layer: 41 of 64 for 16 slots, 26 for 8 slots, 56 for 32 slots.

Burst per turn at L=8, one agent:

| Design | Burst |
|---|---|
| D3 | ~30 ms |
| D5 | ~30 ms |
| D2 | ~0.28 s |
| D1 | ~0.6 s |
| D6 | ~1.0 s |
| D4 | ~1.25 s |

With two agents, add about 30-50%. D1, D2, D4 and D6 assumed 100-170 GB/s, so their bursts are optimistic, D6 and D4 by about 2x. Even the worst case is far cheaper than thinking-ON, which writes 100-500 tokens (3-14 s) per turn. D4's time-averaged throughput is borderline, and K=16 / N=4 fixes it.

**Trainability.**
- D5 is cleanest: exact arm-A start, one layer per lap, no recurrent cache state touched.
- D1 also starts as exact arm A. But the board only gets gradient once alpha leaves zero, and its feedback refiner is very weak.
- D6, D2 and D4 put slots in the sequence with no gate, so step 0 is not arm A. D2 also starts the board off its natural trajectory because of the 0.5 damping and the norm hold.
- D1, D2, D4 and D6 all need the cache shim for HF's in-place copy_ in LinearAttentionLayer (shown in transformers 5.20.2). D5 does not.
- D3's Gumbel routing over frozen layers and D4's three-loss setup with 248k-vocab logits every lap are the most fragile.

**Gain.** D6 has the strongest frozen-backbone evidence (LRT and INTACT, shown in R2/R4) and a full-depth re-read every lap. It is the most likely to clear the +3 bar on the village pilot, though I put that at only 30-40% (suggested). D5's single-depth KV read and 3 sparse read sites cap its gain.

A caveat that applies to every design: training depth is at most 3, and validation depth 4-6 is only 18% of rows (1,558 of 8,675; shown, counted). Even +6 on those rows moves the overall score by only about 1.1 points (suggested). The +3 bar therefore needs gains at depth 3 as well.

**Decoration risk.**
- D2 and D5 have the best controls: an arm trained at one lap only and a hinge.
- D6 lacks an arm trained at L=1 with the same refiner. That is cheap to add.
- D4's Jacobi drafting improves by construction as laps increase, so its per-lap draft curve cannot show whether laps add reasoning.

**Ranking: D6 > D5 > D1 > D2 > D4 > D3.**

I would build D6, with these grafted on:
- D1's zero-init gate, so step 0 is exactly arm A and the gate shows how much signal goes through the board.
- The L=1-trained control arm and hinge from D2/D5.
- D5's halting rule and decision-point placement.
- A Mac burst timing on real hardware before spending anything on LFM.

D5 is the fallback if the measured D6 burst exceeds about 1.5 s per turn with 2 agents.

**Keeping the experiments separate.** I used v1 numbers (the 2M from-scratch village model) only as priors, never as pilot predictions. Qwen3.5-0.8B pilot claims and LFM2.5/tau2 claims are kept apart. All pilot and tau2 gains are untested.

**Plain summary for Ben.** Every design keeps typing speed above your 30 tok/s rule, because the thinking happens in one burst before each reply, not while typing. D6 has the best evidence from other papers that it works. Its pause before each reply is probably about 1 second, not the half second it claims. D5 is the cheapest and safest to build but probably gains less.

judges.label: judge:skeptic

scores.strongest_point: Laps are input-space recurrence: the WHOLE frozen backbone re-reads the 16 slots each lap (6 full-attention reads in Qwen, 10 in LFM) and no frozen layer, MoE or not, is ever fed its own output. That sidesteps the Loop-1L seed-0 failure (shown: B start loss 2.56 vs 0.72, 8 passes 40.1 vs A 48.8, 12 passes 29.6) and LOOM's expert collapse. It also has the closest positive frozen-backbone evidence: LRT's recurrent refiner beats an equal-budget non-recurrent refiner, 56.7 vs 47.5 (shown, R4), and INTACT's progressive re-encoding beats joint construction, 84.4 vs 82.0 (shown). Its controls are the most complete of the six: a pause arm P, a parameter-matched LoRA r32 arm A32, a swap arm and a frozen arm F.
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: The lap update starts as a no-op (W_out zero-init), so recurrence has to grow from zero. The budget is 418 steps x 16 = 6,688 rows of answer-only loss, about 3 tokens per row, roughly 20k loss tokens (suggested, from the train_stage1 defaults and the village answers). Project Newt's 'budget, not architecture' failure is the likely outcome (suggested): only <=5% of the signal went through its loop, and its looped arm tied a compute-matched one-pass LoRA (shown, unreviewed). Its TTFT is under-estimated about 2x (see errors). It also lacks an equal-parameter arm trained at L=1, so P(0 laps) and A32 do not separate 'refiner capacity' from 'recurrence'.
factual_errors: Lap cost: '~170 GB/s ≈ 52 ms' and '16/420 = 38 ms from measured prefill' are both too optimistic (suggested). 420 tok/s is the throughput on a long prompt, where the expert reads are shared across many tokens; a 16-token chunk still reads about 41 of 64 experts per layer, ~8.9 GB. At the effective ~70-80 GB/s that the measured decode implies, a lap is ~110-125 ms. L=8 (9 passes) is then ~1.0-1.1 s with 1 agent and ~1.5 s with 2, against the claimed 0.45/0.7 s.

The step-0 claim 'exactly A + 16 pause tokens' is accurate, but it is not exactly arm A: inserting 16 positions shifts the answer positions. Pause tokens hurt Liu's first-token perplexity, 11.63 vs 10.96 (shown, R4). This needs D4's step-0 'board adds <=0.10 nats' check.
The pilot trains LoRA and refiner jointly, but the LFM recipe has 'no LoRA', so a pilot pass does not transfer cleanly (suggested).

Citations checked against the notes and correct (shown): Flamingo single-middle cross-attention 59.8 vs 70.7; HybridAgent 71.4 vs 88.2; INTACT no-preservation 42.9 vs 78.8; CODI; LoRA parameter count 10.82M.

scores.strongest_point: It has the decisive Newt-style control. C1 is the same parameters and the same 16 slots trained at R=1 only, so it separates recurrence from 'pause tokens + extra LoRA', which is what the stage-1 tie (shown: B +0.40, inside the seed spread, lesion -7.7) shows is needed. Its kill criteria are fixed in advance: swap control >=5 points, R8-R1 >=2, beat C1 by >=2. Slots sit in the sequence, so every upper layer reads them natively and no read gate has to open. The board persists across turns, which directly targets the tau2 failure where the model repeated 'User not found' 10 times (suggested).
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: The laps re-apply frozen band layers to their own output: Qwen 8-11, and at LFM scale 8 MoE layers (16-23). That is arm B's mechanism restricted to the slots. At LFM scale that is exactly the Loop-1L hazard (shown: B fell to 29.6 at 12 passes, past its 1-8 training range) plus frozen-router expert reuse (LOOM/SMELT, shown in models trained to loop). D2 trains R only up to 8 yet must not collapse at 12, and at init the laps already perturb the slots (alpha=0.5 times the frozen band output).
factual_errors: The burst estimate assumes ~150 GB/s. At the ~70-80 GB/s that decode implies, R=8 is ~0.28 s with 1 agent and ~0.4 s with 2, not 145/220 ms (suggested). The claimed 'amortised 31.3 tok/s' assumes 60-token turns. tau2 tool-call turns are often ~30 tokens, which gives ~28 tok/s if bursts are counted. Decode itself still clears 30.
'The Loop-1L failure cannot hit text' is true, but the same failure can hit the board, because the slots still pass repeatedly through the re-run MoE band (suggested).
Checked and correct (shown): 39.5% of validation rows at depth >=3 (3,426/8,675); think-LoRA 1.80M; LFM KV 20 KB per position; INTACT swap drop ~8 (78.8 -> 70.9); tau2 23 vs 30 of 40, p≈0.10.

scores.strongest_point: Its speed arithmetic is the only honest one of the six (suggested, checked): it uses the measured ~67 GB/s, giving ~245 MB and ~3.7 ms per lap and +45 ms TTFT with 2 agents. The Mac work is the simplest, because it reads only the existing layer-18 KV and never forks a conv or DeltaNet state. Its controls are strong: a D1 arm trained and tested at L=1, laps 9-12 inside training, a 'more laps not worse' hinge, swap and zero-board lesions, and a halting rule fixed in advance from oracle headroom. Decision points after <|tool_call_start|> fit tau2.
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: Each lap does very little compute: one attention read over a single fixed layer-11 (Qwen) or layer-18 (LFM) KV, plus one MLP, with the same layer applied to its own output. Answer tokens see the board only through zero-init low-rank cross-attention (Wo=0) at 3-5 sites, which is the Newt and Flamingo 'gate never opens / single site is weak' risk: Flamingo single-site 59.8 vs every-layer 70.7 (shown). The likely result is a near-flat lap curve, or a gate that stays near zero, so it would beat neither A nor B by 3.
factual_errors: 'Qwen3.5-0.8B card tau2 11.6' is not in the research notes. Treat it as untested.
'Every-token laps: 1000/(28.2+8·28.2/40) = 29.5' is correct arithmetic, but it assumes all 40 layers cost the same (suggested).

Unique experts: 64·(1-(63/64)^64)=40.6 is equivalent to the other designs' 64·(1-(60/64)^16)≈41.2 (shown, arithmetic). Decision points with an 'upper-half re-forward ≈38 ms' mid-turn are not specified in the pseudocode (untested).
Checked and correct (shown): 3,426 validation rows at depth >=3; the Shapiro halt head right on 9.1%; PonderNet collapse; Flamingo gate 70.7 vs 66.5.

scores.strongest_point: It is the smallest possible change: 0.14M new parameters, exactly arm A at init (alpha=0), +4-6% compute, and decode cost of about 0.01% (8 extra keys per attention layer). Each lap is a full-depth backbone pass over the slots that reads the whole prompt cache, with feedback in embedding space and RMS rescaling, so no frozen layer is fed its own output. Its code facts check out (shown: in-place copy_ in LinearAttentionLayer; the GDN chunked path takes initial_state=recurrent_state).
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: Laps are coupled only through a rank-64 linear map from final hidden states to embeddings over 8 slots. HybridAgent saw raw or identity hidden-state feedback score far below MLP+residual feedback, 71.4 vs 88.2 (shown), and answers read only the last lap through per-head tanh(alpha) gates that may never open (Newt). There is no C1/pause/parameter-matched control, laps are trained only to 8 while 12 must not collapse, and the designer's own P(pass) is 30%.
factual_errors: The lap cost assumes 100-150 GB/s. At the effective ~70-80 GB/s, a lap reading 5.6 GB takes ~70-80 ms, so 8 laps are ~0.6 s with 1 agent and ~0.9 s with 2, not 0.2-0.45 / 0.3-0.7 s (suggested).

Slot RoPE positions T-1..T+6 overlap or follow the answer positions, which start at T-1. Answer queries therefore attend to keys at the same or later positions, which is off-distribution for RoPE (suggested). This is not discussed.
Checked and correct (shown): arm-A LoRA 10,822,656; 1,558 validation rows at depth 4-6; training depth 0-3.

scores.strongest_point: It measures decoration most directly: the frozen head decodes the draft at every lap, so it counts wrong->right and right->wrong flips per lap. It adds a check ablation (chk set to its mean) and a step-0 'untrained board costs <=0.10 nats' test. The corruption curriculum (swap in a wrong entity or ID) targets the wrong-argument errors that make up about half of tau-bench failures (suggested).
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: Six interacting new parts must all train on ~20k answer tokens: refiner, verifier, Jacobi shift, taps, gates and the corruption curriculum. It also needs 248k-vocab logits per slot per lap. The 'draft' is the final answer, not an intermediate hop, so it does not provide the hop-per-lap mechanism the depth axis needs. Jacobi shifting buys little for village answers with a median of 3 tokens. It has the heaviest Mac burst: 32 tokens through 40 layers per lap, ~11.9 GB.
factual_errors: TTFT: at ~75 GB/s a lap is ~160 ms, so 8 laps are ~1.3 s with 1 agent and ~1.9 s with 2 (suggested), at the top of or above the claimed 0.8-1.2 s.

It cites the v1 'lastloss' finding (v1 village model only) as support, but trains with per-lap draft CE, which is deep supervision. TaH measured per-lap next-token loss at -4.3 vs final-lap only (shown, R3). That evidence argues against its own loss.
'Jacobi has a fixed point, so no collapse at 12' does not hold, because the refiner state b keeps moving whenever v_seq<1 (suggested).
'Village SE ~0.5 at n=8,675' is binomial noise only. Seed spread is ~1.7 points range for A (shown) and dominates, though the 3-seed SE is similar (~0.5-0.55).

scores.strongest_point: It is very cheap on the Mac (~4 ms per lap, decode ~34.8 tok/s), it is honest that its own prior is weak, and its D-fixed control (M=1) plus route histograms would show quickly whether routing is decoration.
scores.fatal_or_biggest_flaw: It adds a second thing that can be decoration, the router, on top of the laps, with no evidence behind it. Untying routers moved loss by <0.01 nats (shown, Tying the Loop), and trained loops re-pick the same experts (SMELT, shown). It feeds a layer-15 hidden state into frozen layers 3 and 7, an off-depth input, and uses Gumbel Switch routing plus two upper passes on 418 steps. It has no non-recurrent (R=1-trained) control.
factual_errors: The per-lap MoE read is computed as if all 16 slots go to one layer (41 experts, 218 MB). Split over 4 pool layers at ~4 slots each, the union is ~4x14 ≈ 57 experts, ~300 MB (suggested). This is a minor under-estimate and still cheap.
The Liu et al. figure is correctly 'KV-cache read 26.76 vs last-layer read 23.20' (shown, R4). It does not support 'each lap picks its depth', which is the design's own inference (suggested).

ideas_worth_grafting: From D2: add arm C1 to the winner's pilot. C1 is the same refiner, slots and LoRA trained and tested at L=1. This is the Newt-style equal-parameter, non-recurrent control. P (0 laps) and A32 (parameter-matched LoRA) do not separate 'refiner capacity' from 'recurrence'. Make 'STS@8 - C1 >= 2' a pass mark fixed in advance.

From D4: decode the answer with the frozen head after every lap and log per-lap wrong->right / right->wrong flips by depth. This makes decoration directly visible at almost no cost. Also take D4's step-0 check (an untrained board costs <=0.10 nats vs no board), because STS at init is A + 16 pause tokens, not exactly A.

From D5: re-do the TTFT estimate with the measured ~67-79 GB/s, not 150-170 GB/s; expect ~1-1.5 s per turn at L=8 with 2 agents. Keep K=8 / L=4 as fallbacks. Adopt D5's rule fixed in advance: no halt unless held-out oracle headroom is >=2 points. Add decision points after <|tool_call_start|> for tau2.
From D2 and D5: an optional detached hinge relu(CE(L+k) - sg(CE(L))), so that more laps cannot be worse. Run it as an ablation, not as the default, so it cannot manufacture a rising curve.

From D2 and D6: a budget test, one seed each of A and the winner at 418 vs 1,254 steps, to tell Newt's 'budget, not architecture' failure from a wrong design. Given ~20k loss-bearing answer tokens in 418 steps, run it before declaring the design dead.
From D3 and D5: before any LFM training, a Mac pre-check with no training. Measure lap-to-lap expert-set overlap (Jaccard) and the time of one 16-slot pass at 12k context with 2 agents.

From D1: a smoke test as gate 0. Gates off must give logits identical to stock HF, and cached generation must equal a full re-forward at L=1/4/8. Use an out-of-place cache subclass, because HF 5.20.2 LinearAttentionLayer uses in-place copy_ (shown). Keep D1's parameter-free expected-embedding feedback, softmax(lm_head(h)/τ)·W_emb, as the fallback if fed-back states go off-manifold.
judges.rationale:
I scored as a skeptic. On the stage-1 Qwen pilot (village task, kept separate from v1, premonition's from-scratch village model), the bar is >=70.1 validation: beat B (67.12) and A (66.72) by >=3 on a 3-seed mean (shown). Seed spread is ~1.2-1.7 points (shown), B's re-run loop bought +0.40 (shown), and the 1-pass lesion (-7.7) is expected for any trained loop and proves nothing (suggested, McLeish).

The closest outside evidence is mostly negative or small:
- Project Newt: a LoRA loop on a frozen Qwen3.5-family hybrid tied a compute-matched 1-pass LoRA, with <=5% of the signal going through the loop (shown, unreviewed).
- Frozen-backbone latent methods give +1 to +5 (shown, R2/R4).
- Coda-Forno: a frozen base capped GSM8K at 22-24 vs 38.5 for a trainable base (shown).

The pilot budget is also tiny: 6,688 rows with ~3-token answer-only loss (suggested). My honest P(PASS) is roughly 10-20% for the best design and lower for the rest, below every designer's self-estimate (25-40%).

All six run laps once per turn, never per token. Decode therefore stays at ~34-35 tok/s with 2 agents and every design passes the speed gate (suggested, arithmetic). The real cost is TTFT, which D1, D2 and D6 under-estimate about 2x by assuming 100-170 GB/s instead of the ~70-80 GB/s that the measured 18 ms decode implies.

The Loop-1L seed-0 results are early (56 steps), on LFM2.5 with M_tool, and separate from the pilot. They show that re-feeding frozen MoE layers their own output knocks the model off its function and collapses past the trained lap range (shown). That count is against D2 and D5 at LFM scale (they re-run band layers on the slots) and in favour of D6 and D1, whose laps re-enter at the embedding layer.

D6 ranks first: it has the strongest positive frozen-backbone evidence (LRT recurrence vs equal budget, INTACT progressive re-encoding), it avoids self-feeding layers, and it has the most controls. Its biggest weakness is a zero-init recurrence on a starved budget; graft D2's C1 control onto it.

D2 is a close second. It has the best decisive control (C1) and a native in-sequence read, but its MoE band is re-run on its own output and it is trained only to 8 laps.

D5 is third: the cheapest and most honest on speed, with good controls, but each lap is a single layer with a gated low-rank read, so a flat curve is likely.

D1 is simple and safe but lacks controls and feeds back through a weak rank-64 linear path. D4 measures decoration best but is too complex for the budget, uses per-lap supervision that TaH found harmful (-4.3, shown), and has the heaviest burst. D3 adds an unproven router as a second source of decoration.

No claim about tau2 gain from any design is better than untested. The 23->30 gap is 7 tasks, inside the n=40 noise (p≈0.10, shown).

attacks.label: attack:pilot:halt
fatal: F1. The PASS bar is above every capacity lever measured on this pilot, and the design's own forecast misses it. [Qwen pilot] To pass, D's 3-seed validation mean must reach 70.12 (B 67.12 + 3; A 66.72) [shown]. Nothing measured so far has added more than about 2 points: (a) B, which re-runs layers 8-11 at every position, gave +0.40 [shown]; (b) Qwen3.5-2B + LoRA, a backbone 2.5x larger, scored 69.81, which is +2.03 over A seed 0 and still BELOW the bar [shown, 1 seed]; (c) running more steps (537 vs 418) gave -0.32 [shown]. D adds 3.56M parameters, +33% over A's 10,822,656 trainable (result_a.json) [shown], and would have to beat a 2B model. The design forecasts 69.1 for itself. A's seed sd is 0.93 [shown], so the SE of a 3-seed mean is about 0.54, and a true mean of 69.1 would clear 70.12 about 3% of the time [suggested arithmetic]. The design's per-depth predictions also don't add up. With 39.5% of rows at depth >=3, a gain of +5 there contributes only +2.0 overall. Its '+3.0 for 8 laps vs 1' therefore also needs about +4.3 on the 2,057 depth-2 rows [shown counts].

F2. The laps aim at rows the training data never asks them to solve. [Qwen pilot data] By construction, training questions have depth <=3 (scheduler docstring). I counted 5,703 / 33,800 / 28,480 / 18,255 rows at depths 0-3 and none at 4 or more. Validation has 1,558 rows (18%) at depths 4-6 [shown]. The '-8 depth' probe switches MAX_DEPTH to the validation setting, so it measures extrapolation beyond the trained depth (probes.py) [shown]. Depth closely tracks how many evidence lines a question needs: the mean is 1.25 / 1.93 / 2.95 / 3.76 / 4.59 lines at depths 1-5 [shown, 20 shards]. 'Hop t needs lap t' fits the chain-type banks, and in training those never need more than 3 lines. where_before at depth 3 needs exactly 3 lines in 88% of rows (1,804 / 2,047), and plan_get needs 2-3. 80% of the training rows that need 4 or more lines are counting questions (3,092 / 3,842), which are parallel lookups, not chains [shown]. The two chain banks hold 44% of arm A's validation errors (plan_get 715 + where_before 578 out of 2,955), and 48% of their rows are at depth 4-6 [shown]. Under answer-only CE, nothing trains lap 4 or later to make hop 4 or later. The hinge relu(CE(L+4) - sg CE(L)) is exactly zero for a flat curve, so it rewards the board for not changing after hop 3 [suggested]. In the literature, a LoRA loop on a frozen 0.5B needed exact per-lap labels and still extrapolated only about 1.5x beyond its supervised depth (Shapiro, R1) [shown]. The in-range pool is small. where_before plus plan_get at depth <=3 is about 1,044 validation rows with roughly 430-500 errors at A's dev-level accuracy (49% / 64%). Fixing a generous third of them is worth +1.5 to +2 overall [suggested].
serious: S1. The 'damped' update has no fixed point. The pseudocode describes u = block(z) as 'attn + MLP, residual', so z + γ(u - z) = z + 0.5·(attn(LN z) + MLP(...)). That is a half-scaled re-application of a frozen pre-norm residual layer, and a fixed point would need the layer's output to be zero, which never happens. There is no norm clamp, so ||z|| grows every lap. The backbone reads the board through rms(z), so each lap's visible change shrinks roughly as ||Δ||/||z_t|| (a flat curve), or z drifts along the layer's dominant output direction once past the trained range [suggested]. The same class of failure has been seen: [Loop-1L LFM] a self-fed re-run trained with random 1-8 passes scored 41.4 / 43.8 / 40.7 / 29.6 at 1 / 4 / 8 / 12 passes [shown, seed 0, 162 turns]; [lit] LOOM reports hidden-variance growth [shown]; [village v1] state change per loop fell 6.7x, then 1.8, then 0.14 by loop 8 [shown]. The claim '16 laps won't collapse because the operator is tied and damped' is untested, and the mechanism argues against it.

S2. The slots start symmetric, which invites collapse. All 16 slots begin as h_11[dec] + z0 at the same RoPE position, pass through the same frozen projections and read the same KV. They differ only by z0, whose init scale is never given. If z0 is small next to the residual stream, every slot gets the same attention and the same gradient, so the board acts like one slot (K_eff ≈ 1) [suggested]. [lit] Latents overlap 0.987 at Qwen3-0.6B (Coda-Forno), and SoftCoT and EBM-CoT latents collapse [shown]. [village v1] The decoder ignored its 4 registers [shown]. At lap 0 the board is also the very state the answer position already holds, so its only new content is the sum of the γΔ updates.

S3. Any gain is as likely to come from parameters and learning rate as from laps. The new parameters train at lr 1e-3, 5x A's LoRA rate (the 2e-4 default in train_stage1.py, not overridden in run_box.sh) [shown, code]. A is under-trained at 418 steps: its loss is still falling (0.20 to 0.14 over the last ~130 steps) and where_before dev is 49% [shown]. The design's D1 control (trained at L=1) is not a clean parameter control. That would be an L=0 board: same sites, same LR, z = z0 + h, no laps. [lit] In Newt's 0.8B follow-up, the margin over a 1-pass LoRA came from the parameters of its 1-pass column [shown, single author]. On the judges' claim: a zero-init Wo under Adam opens within tens of steps, because Adam's per-element step is about lr whatever the gradient size [suggested]. Newt's gates were stuck at saturation, not at zero. So 'the gate stays shut' is the weaker risk. The stronger one is that Wo opens and carries a signal that doesn't depend on laps.

S4. D's most plausible gain would not depend on laps, so it would fail the slope half of PASS. Sixteen parallel slots can help the counting banks in lap 1 (count_at 46%, count_held 57%, about 300 errors) [shown accuracies]. That raises the score and flattens the lap curve [suggested]. [village v1] With 16 registers that the decoder did use (zeroing them cost 5.4 points), validation was still 2.6 points worse than base over 4 seeds [shown].

S5. Overthinking costs points. A gets about 5,720 validation rows right [shown]. [lit] On Ouro-1.7B, a second lap broke 2.1% of correct predictions (TaH) [shown]. Breaking just 1% of A's correct rows costs about 0.7 points, so D would need to fix about 320 rows net, around 11% of all of A's errors [suggested]. Meanwhile about a third of A's errors are in held-out rule-family rows (1,497 rows at ~37%), and depth-0/1 rows make up 36.8% of validation, where the design itself predicts about zero gain [shown counts].

S6. Each lap reads one fixed layer with one reused frozen layer. Every lap reads only layer 11's KV (2 KV heads x 256). [lit] DCA scored 26.8 reading the full KV vs 23.2 reading last-layer activations [shown, a different setting]. Newt on the same backbone (Qwen3.5-0.8B, 30M tokens) found loop-3 minus its own loop-1 of -0.002 / -0.005 / -0.020 [shown, single author]. [Qwen pilot] At the decision token the backbone still has three full-attention layers after layer 11 (15, 19, 23). So lap 1 amounts to one more layer-11 read at one position, which is less compute than B's 8 extra layer passes at every position, and those gave +0.4 [shown].

S7. Noise and how depth is sliced. The design quotes a binomial SE of about 0.5, but seed spread on this pilot is 1.2-1.7 points and dominates [shown]. 'depth' is confounded with question type: compare_count's 677 rows at depth 3-5 already score 92% [shown]. So '>= +5 at depth >= 3' would partly be a statement about question mix. fatal: F1. A pilot PASS does not license the LFM block, because the two laps differ in exactly the parts most likely to break. At LFM, the lap is layer 18: attention plus a frozen 64-expert MoE with a frozen sigmoid router that uses expert_bias [shown, HF modeling_lfm2_moe.py and config.json]. D5's LFM block LoRA covers attention only: 212,992 params, with zero on the FFN [shown, design §2 arithmetic checked]. HF stores the experts as 3-D Parameters (gate_up_proj, down_proj), so ordinary PEFT target_modules cannot reach them [shown, code]. The pilot lap (Qwen3.5 layer 11) has a dense MLP with its own LoRA: 221,184 of its 401,408 block-LoRA params [shown, arithmetic]. So the half of the lap that the pilot trains is frozen at scale. The router, which is the part most likely to misbehave on self-fed slots, is never exercised in the pilot. Evidence on that risk: LOOM saw expert-selection collapse and hidden-variance growth past 2 loops [shown, from-scratch MoE, per R1 notes]. Loop-1L B started at training loss 2.56 vs 0.72 and fell to 29.6% at 12 passes [shown]. The pilot also has 1 decision point per village row. tau2 has a median of 14 assistant turns per episode (10th-90th pct 10-19), and 83 of 299 tool turns carry text before the call, which fires the mid-turn trigger [shown, lfm25_think_results.json]. A village pass therefore predicts little about LFM [suggested].

F2. At scale there is no headroom over arm A that the tau2 eval could detect, and no LFM pass mark is set. Thinking-OFF lost 9 tasks to too_many_errors loops: it repeated a failed call such as 'User not found' 10 times [shown, RESULTS-mac-lfm25.md]. That OFF arm forces an empty think block onto a model whose template always opens '<think>' [shown, chat_template.jinja]. This looks like a format or repetition failure, which arm A's LoRA (trained on 205 error_recovery chats [shown, stats.json]) or a one-line prompt rule may remove with no board at all [suggested]. If A recovers about 5 of the 7 tasks, the most D can add is about 2 tasks [suggested]. The tau2 eval cannot resolve that: 40 tasks x 1 trial has roughly +/-7 points SD [suggested, scoreboard notes; task 0 flipped between runs, shown]. A paired 3-point D-A difference needs about 7.84*0.25/0.03^2 ≈ 2,200 task-trials per arm at 25% discordance, about 180 Mac-hours at the measured ~5 min per task with 2 agents [suggested arithmetic]. tau2 can only detect 'closes most of the 17.5-point gap' (about 64 paired task-trials). D5's §3 gives no pass mark for the LFM stage [shown]. As written, no outcome of the scale-up can show that the board beats A by >=3.

F3. The LFM training signal is off-domain and nearly the same as arm A's. The only per-turn gold calls are in the 1,792 Claude-written personal-assistant chats: 15 email, calendar and file tools, a mean of 7.9 messages and 3.3 assistant turns, about 2.4k tokens, and Loop-1L uses max-len 4096 [shown, stats.json and loop1l.py; token count suggested]. tau2 retail looks different: a ~4.8k-token policy-plus-tools system prompt, and a median of 6.4k tokens of context per turn (p90 9.4k, max 12.5k) [shown]. So at test the board reads layer-18 KV unlike anything it was trained on [suggested]. 'Keep teacher turns that match gold, then KL on action tokens' makes the KL roughly equal to CE on gold, since the teacher's argmax is the gold call. The only extra signal comes from the minority of turns where ON is right and OFF is wrong [suggested]. That is the answer-only setting in which B gained +0.4 on village [shown] and Coconut without a curriculum scored at the no-CoT level [shown, R2]. Teacher-forced gold histories also never show the model its own repeated failing calls, and those loops are most of the gap [suggested].
serious: S1. At LFM the self-fed lap probably drifts and its slots probably collapse. The update z <- z + γ(Block(z) - z) is an Euler step along layer 18's residual update. A pre-norm layer's update has roughly constant size whatever ‖z‖ is, so z drifts along the mean update direction. ‖Δz‖/‖z‖ then falls roughly like 1/t, which looks like the v1 village model's 'fixed point by lap 3' (that was a different, from-scratch model) without actually converging [suggested]. The sites read rms(z), so they see a direction that settles within a few laps, and the lap curve goes flat [untested]. The init of z0 is not specified. If z0 is identical across slots, the 16 slots stay exact copies: inputs, the tied operator, slot attention and the gradients are all slot-symmetric, so K=16 acts as K=1 [shown, by construction]. If z0 is merely small next to ‖h_18‖, the result is nearly the same; the Loop-1L code notes that 'h has a large scale' [suggested]. Latent overlap of 0.987 was seen in Coda-Forno [shown, R4]. The 'more laps must not be worse' hinge is satisfied by an idempotent block, so it rewards a flat curve, not a rising one [suggested].

S2. Most of the speed headroom disappears at real tau2 context. bench.py measured with a short prompt [shown]. Decoding in tau2 happens at a median of 6.4k tokens of context (p75 8.1k) [shown]. Each decoded token reads KV of 10 layers x 2 KB x context, which is 131 MB per agent at 6.4k. For 2 agents that adds about 4.0 ms per step at the ~65 GB/s the bench implies [suggested arithmetic]. At 6.4k the base runs about 31.0 tok/s and D5 (+1.15 ms) about 30.0. At 8.1k the base is about 30.0 and D5 about 29.0. The claimed 5.1 ms of headroom is about 1 ms in practice. Time to first token is fine. In the thinking-ON run, per-turn agent time has a median of 38 s, and a fit gives 10.8 s + 3.43 ms per prompt token + 22.4 ms per completion token (R^2 0.51) [shown, my regression]. That points to a full re-prefill every turn [suggested], so D5's +45-70 ms per turn is under 0.3%.

S3. On this harness, thinking ON costs only about 15% of wall-clock. Reasoning totals about 14.5k chars per episode [shown], roughly 3.9k tokens, or about 87 s at 22.4 ms per token, out of a 600 s median episode [suggested]. Re-prefill at about 22 s per turn is the larger cost [suggested]. So at scale D5 competes with 'thinking ON plus a fixed prompt cache', which keeps 30/40 [shown] and probably saves more time than D5 does [suggested].

S4. Train/serve format and cache mismatch. The template's generation prompt ends with '<|im_start|>assistant
<think>'. History assistant turns with empty thinking are rendered with no think tags. The Mac OFF arm appends '<think>
</think>
'. Loop-1L's render() writes '<think></think>' (no newlines) into every turn, history included [all shown]. So the decision token, h_18[dec] (the board's init) and the positions of the history boards all differ between training and the Mac [effect untested]. With a full re-prefill each turn, mlx must rebuild about 14 boards per request using exactly the training segmentation; otherwise history tokens see no board [suggested]. The mid-turn 'upper-half re-forward' would advance the short-conv caches (mlx ArraysCache, HF conv_states) twice unless they are snapshotted [suggested]. None of the mlx-lm work exists yet [shown, not in repo]: a custom lfm2_moe forward split at layer 18; slot attention over cache.keys[..., :offset] without appending to the cache; a per-token board gather at 5 sites; batched-server support; and PEFT-to-mlx LoRA conversion.

S5. The lap is trained in bf16 but deployed in 4-bit. Training is bf16 and tau2 runs on mlx affine 4-bit (about 4.5 bits per weight) [shown]. Eight laps of the quantized layer 18 compound the quantization error inside the board, and the board's effect on the answer enters through a small learned Wo [untested]. D5 plans no parity check.

S6. The JOLT+ RL stage cannot run as specified. rlaif is a Qwen3-1.7B LoRA RL loop on a personal-assistant sandbox, with no tau2 environment, no LFM support and no board [shown, rlaif/SPEC.md]. Sonnet is priced at $2/$10 per M tokens [shown, grader.py]. Rollouts with the board need one of two routes. (a) HF generate on Vast, where Lfm2MoeExperts loops over experts in Python [shown, code], so 600 s-class episodes cost A100-hours. (b) mlx 4-bit on the Mac with bf16 updates, which gives a large GRPO ratio mismatch between rollout and training policies [suggested]. JOLT+'s teacher shares the student's weights, so stage 2 has no fixed anchor; INTACT without its preservation KL fell from 78.8 to 42.9 [shown, R4]. Fixed L=8 drops the random laps and the hinge, so the lap curve is no longer trained [suggested]. RL gains on a frozen backbone were -0.1 to +4.5 [shown, INTACT math]. A Sonnet judge invites an input-independent 'please the grader' board, the kind of latent collapse seen in SoftCoT and EBM-CoT [shown, R4].

S7. The teacher thinks hardest on the turns that neither the metric nor the distillation looks at. Reasoning is longest on text turns (median 790-1,120 chars, mean 1,500-1,750) and shortest on tool-call turns (median 300-350) [shown]. 13% of turns exceed 2,000 chars, and they hold 54% of all reasoning [shown]. M_tool scores text turns only as 'made no call', and action-anchored KL on gold-matched turns concentrates on tool turns [suggested]. D5's lap budget is 16 slots x 8 laps x 1 layer = 128 slot-layer updates, against roughly 500+ tokens x 40 layers on those long turns, i.e. under 1% [suggested]. On long self-generated traces, latent methods keep only about 25-40% of CoT accuracy [shown, Tale of Two Regimes, 1-1.5B math].

S8. The training budget does not fit this week. Loop-1L's full spec came to about 7.7 A100-hours and was cut to 25% of the data (56 steps) to fit $3 [shown]. D5 at LFM needs arms A, D and D1 x >=2 seeds on 6-12k-token retail sequences, about 2-3x the tokens per chat, roughly $5-15 [suggested], against a few dollars of credit [shown, brief].

fatal: F1. The +3 bar is above anything this pilot has produced, the design's own forecast included. PASS needs a 3-seed validation mean of at least 70.12 (B 67.12 + 3; A is 66.72) [shown]. Three anchors: (a) the 2.5x larger backbone, A2 = Qwen3.5-2B + LoRA, scored 69.81, only +2.03 over seed-matched A [shown, 1 seed]; (b) B, which re-runs the same band 8-11 three times at every position, gave +0.40 on validation and +1.57 on dev, with all 3 seeds positive on dev [shown]; (c) the design itself predicts about 68.9 (+1.8 over the best of A and B) and gives itself a 25% chance [stated in design-board.md]. So 16 slots plus 1.80M think-LoRA parameters (+16.7% over A's 10.82M) would have to beat a 2B model on held-out data, and the cheaper version of the same idea (B) bought +0.4.

F2. The 'one hop per lap' story targets depth that training never contains, and depth is not where most validation errors are. I counted the village files [shown]: train has depth 0/1/2/3 = 5,703 / 33,800 / 28,480 / 18,255 and nothing deeper; dev also stops at 3. Validation has 1,558 of 8,675 questions (18.0%) at depth 4-6. With answer-only loss on questions of depth 3 or less, no gradient asks a lap to do a 4th to 6th hop. The best published hop extrapolation is about 1.5x the supervised depth, and that needed per-lap state labels (Shapiro 2608.11233) [shown there; untested here]. Arm A seed 0 by bank [shown, result_a.json]: rule-family rows (1,497) score about 37% against 71.9% for the 7,178 non-rule rows. The worst banks are what_if 13.1%, rule_place 31.0%, where_before 33.5% and plan_get 37.8%, all new templates or rules, and looping does not add knowledge (R1 notes: Capo, NQ) [shown in those papers]. Upper-bound arithmetic [computed]: +10 points on every depth 4-6 row gives +1.8 overall, and the design's own +6 on all 3,426 depth-3+ rows gives +2.4. Both fall short of the +3.4 over A that PASS needs.

F3. The training signal is about 150x below the closest published negative result. 418 steps x 16 rows x 4.10 answer tokens (Qwen tokenizer on dev, median 3 including EOS) is about 27k loss-bearing tokens [computed]. The design's '7M tokens' counts prompt tokens (I get 7.6M) [computed]. Project Newt, on a frozen Qwen3.5-family hybrid with about 4M loss-bearing tokens [shown, author's README, re-fetched]: no looped arm beat a compute-matched 1-pass LoRA, and at most 5% of the signal went through the loop (mix weights 0.977/0.973). Its Qwen3.5-0.8B follow-up with 30M tokens gave loop-3 minus loop-1 of about 0 [shown per R1 notes, not re-fetched]. Coconut trained on the answer only, with no curriculum, scored 14.4 against 16.5 for no-CoT [shown]. With this budget the cheapest thing the optimiser can find is 'slots = extra LoRA capacity, laps idle' [suggested].
serious: S1. The rise with laps will be manufactured, so that half of PASS is cheap and tells you nothing. Under loss = ce[-1] + 0.1*hinge, lap 1's readout gets a direct loss only in R=1 steps (10%, about 42 of 418). 45% of steps run at R 6 or 8. A rising curve then comes from under-trained low laps, not from better high laps. Precedents: B's 1-pass lesion costs 7.7 points while B ties A [shown]. McLeish: trained at 32 laps and tested at 1, GSM8K 6.4 against 37.1 for the parent [shown]. The village model v1 (premonition's own, risk only, its numbers are not used for the pilot): lastloss gave a steeper 2-to-8 gain (+13.0 against +7.9) with an endpoint that is not better (47.5 against 44.7, p about 0.16) [shown]. My prediction [untested]: R8 - R1 >= 2 and R12 >= R8 - 1 both pass, R8 - R4 < 0.5 (a fixed point by lap 3-4: Closing-the-Loop sees at most 0.01 nats past lap 4, Ouro peaks at 4), and D2@R8 is within 1.5 points of B.

S2. Step 0 is not arm A, and R=1 is not 'the slots run normally'. With every LoRA at zero, the answer already reads 16 extra positions at all 24 layers. The gate is missing at the attention reads (3/7/11/15/19/23) and at the DeltaNet states: the 16 slots are the last writes into the delta-rule memories at layers 12-14, 16-18 and 20-22, right before the answer, and they can overwrite prompt associations the answer depends on [suggested]. Even at R=1, layer 12 receives normalise(Z0 + 0.5*(band(Z0) - Z0)) rescaled to the layer-8 norm rms(Z0), a half-applied band at the wrong depth's norm that layer 12 has never seen [shown by the pseudocode; size untested]. At R=8 with alpha 0.5 the band is applied to its own output about 4 times (R*alpha), which is the mechanism behind B's failures. The design calls this 'near normal hidden states'; that is unsupported. Memorilla's random-init memory tokens made a frozen agent worse than no memory (15.3 against 18.6) [shown there].

S3. No structural edge over B at the lap counts that matter. With 3 passes, B's question and answer tokens already make 3 question-directed reads at full-attention layer 11, against 1 for A, and B tied A on validation [shown]. D2 at R=3 gives the board the same 3 reads at layer 11, plus the 3 DeltaNet layers reading a prompt state that is restored identically every lap. Its upper stack (12-23) runs once, against B's answer tokens getting 3 passes of the band themselves. The extra reads at R=4-8 only pay off for hops 4+, which F2 shows are untrained [suggested].

S4. Noise and harness confounds sit at the scale of the margin. The same arm (A), seed (0) and step count (418) gave 67.78 and 65.94 on two runs [shown: RESULTS-stage1 table versus the probes2 run]. That is a rerun spread of 1.84 points, and the stage-1 seeds ran on mixed Vast and PC GPUs. D2 must left-pad in training to put the slots after each prompt, while stage-1 trained with right padding (train_stage1.py: right_pad in training, left_pad in eval) [shown]. Reusing the old A and B numbers would confound the comparison.

S5. The spec leaves out which position predicts the first answer token. In the pseudocode, CE(run(ha...), ans) only gives logits at the answer positions, so token a1 is either unsupervised or predicted by the last slot. 23.7% of validation answers are a single token (yes/no/numbers/names) [computed]. If slot 16 predicts a1, the 'board read through attention' story does not hold for a quarter of the set. If nothing predicts it, the decisive token is never trained.

S6. The swap control cannot separate 'laps compute' from 'slots hold a re-encoded question'. A board from another question breaks either way (INTACT: swap cost 7.9 points, shuffle only 1.8 [shown]). So swap >= 5 shows the board is read, not that laps matter. Only the C1 comparison tests the laps, and C1 is not in Ben's PASS.

S7. The pilot cannot test the LFM risks, so a pass would not carry over. The Qwen band 8-11 is dense, and 4 of its 4 layers read the whole prompt (3 DeltaNet with a compressed prompt state, plus attention at 11). The LFM band 16-23 is all MoE with a frozen router, and 6 of its 8 layers are short convs with cache 3, so slots there see only the 2 previous positions. Only layers 18 and 22 read the prompt each lap [shown, configs]. Loop-1L seed 0 [shown, 56 steps]: B's start loss was 2.56 against 0.72, and B fell to 29.6 at 12 passes against 40.7 at 8 (162-turn subset), past its 1-8 training range. Frozen-router expert reuse across visits is shown only in models trained to loop (SMELT, LOOM). D2 trains R only up to 8.

S8. Implementation risk could cause silent decoration. The work needs a custom BoardCache (HF's DeltaNet and conv caches update in place, so autograd breaks), gradients through the restored DeltaNet initial_state into the prompt pass R times, a hand-built 4-D SDPA mask with left padding, and R upper-stack forks per step. A dropped gradient path produces exactly the 'board ignored' result with no error [suggested; Shapiro: gates folded into a projection 'fail silently' (shown)].

Add depth 4-6 training rows with probes.write_training_data(('difficulty',), n, OUT_DIR), which exists on the Loop-1L branch, or at least pre-register the validation depth 4-6 slice (n=1,558) as the place the gain must appear.
