Give D2 a denser signal that A cannot use: uniform-weight per-lap CE on every lap 1..R (Ouro uniform prior, 2610.00673 smoothed exit), and if the generator exposes hop chains, intermediate-hop targets for lap k (Shapiro's per-lap labels, then outcome-only steps) [untested here].

For S1: replace 'ce[-1] + 0.1 hinge' with equal-weight per-lap CE, so a weak lap 1 cannot be used to fake a rising curve. Write C1 into PASS: D2@R8 - C1@R1 >= 2, D2@R1 >= C1@R1 - 1 (no low-lap damage), and R8 - R4 >= 1 (the gain is not finished by lap 4).

For S2: make step 0 equal arm A exactly. Use a per-layer learned additive attention-logit bias on slot keys for non-slot queries, initialised at -10. Scale each slot's DeltaNet write strength (beta) by tanh(g) with g=0, so slots cannot overwrite prompt memory at init. Make lap 1 an ordinary forward (alpha_1 = 1, no rescale), damp only laps 2+, and renormalise to the measured rms of lap 1's output, not rms(Z0). Check that the zero-LoRA answer NLL equals A's to within 0.01 nats before any training.

For S4 and S5: re-run A and B in the new left-padded harness, on the same GPU type, with 3 seeds each. State that a fixed ' [answer]' token after the board predicts a1, so every answer token reads the board through attention.

For S6: add a lap-swap control. Score the R=8 answer with the board computed by the same weights at R=1; the drop is the work of laps 2-8. Also run a constant (mean) board at R=8 and the per-lap ||Z_r - Z_{r-1}||/||Z0|| trace.

For S7 (LFM, separate from the pilot): before any scale-up training, run zero-training diagnostics on the Mac with mlx. Measure expert-set overlap between lap 1 and lap k at layers 16-23, and the change in answer NLL after 1/4/8/12 slot laps with zero adapters. Consider a band that contains more attention layers, and train R up to 12 if 12 must not collapse.
attacks.kill_experiment: One seed, free on Ben's PC (RTX 5070 Ti), about 1.5 GPU-hours, no money. Seed 0, 418 steps, same harness and data order: train D2 exactly as specified, plus C1 (the same model trained at R=1 only). Score the full validation set (8,675 questions) at R = 1/2/4/8/12, split by depth 0-3 and depth 4-6 (n=1,558). Fix these thresholds in advance. The attack is RIGHT if any of these hold: (a) D2@R8 < 68.5 (the other two seeds would then need to average at least 70.9, more than 2 SD above any arm's observed seed spread); (b) D2@R8 - C1@R1 < 1.0; (c) R8 - R1 >= 2 while D2@R1 < C1@R1 - 1, so the rise comes from damaged low laps; (d) R8 - R4 < 0.5; (e) D2's gain over C1 on depth 4-6 is no larger than its gain on depth 0-3. The attack is WRONG if D2@R8 >= 70.5, D2@R8 - C1@R1 >= 2, R8 - R4 >= 1 and the depth 4-6 gain exceeds the depth 0-3 gain. A 10-minute precursor with no training (a frozen forward on 1,000 validation questions, CPU or PC) settles S2 on its own: with zero LoRAs, if answer NLL with slots at R=1 minus NLL without slots is above 0.05 nats, step 0 is not A; if the per-lap change ratio falls below 0.05 by lap 3, the board is at a fixed point.

attacks.label: attack:pilot:contrarian
fatal: F1. The 3-point bar is out of reach on this metric. Village model only (Qwen3.5-0.8B stage 1). PASS needs a mean of at least 70.12 on validation, which is B's 67.12 + 3 [shown, RESULTS-stage1 three-seed table]. That is +3.4 over A's 66.72, and it is above the Qwen3.5-2B LoRA arm at the same 418 steps (A2 69.81, seed 0) [shown]. So a 0.8B plus an 11.6M refiner must beat a backbone 2.5x larger. That backbone gained only +2.0, and B's 3x middle loop gained +0.4 [shown]. Where validation loses points (computed from backbone/results/probes2/result_a.json, arm A seed 0, 34.1 points of error in total) [shown]: (a) Q8 'rule' questions are all depth 1 (623 rows): dev 98.2 vs val 43.5. Q7 'what-if' (251 rows, depth 1-3): dev 77.1 vs val 6.0. Together they cost 6.0 points of the dev-validation gap and hold 6.8 points of error. Every validation row has an unseen template (template_seen=False for all 8,675), and on Pdepth, where templates are seen, Q7/Q8 score 79/98 [shown]. So this is a template/answer-format failure that laps cannot fix [suggested]. (b) By D6's own logic (~0 gain on 1-hop), the 36.8% of validation rows at depth <= 1 contribute nothing [shown composition: depth 0/1/2/3/4/5/6 = 6.2/30.6/23.7/21.5/13.5/4.2/0.3%]. (c) The multi-hop pool is mainly Q4 where_before plus Q12 plan_get: 2,552 rows, 29.4% of validation, 15.9 points of error [shown]. Reaching +3.4 from them alone needs +11.6 points on those qtypes [computed]. D6's own forecast (+5 on 3+-hop, ~0 on 1-hop, STS@8 = B+3.0, P(PASS) 0.4) puts the expected value right on the bar, so even if every assumption holds it passes about half the time [suggested]. Nothing measured in this repo has moved 0.8B validation by more than ~2 points [shown].

F2. Gradient starvation: the LoRA takes the signal before the refiner can learn. Village model. The budget is 418 x 16 = 6,688 rows (7.8% of one epoch) [shown]. With the real Qwen3.5 tokenizer, a random 6,688-row train sample has 27,696 answer-loss tokens including EOS, mean 4.14 [shown, counted]. Only 1,463 of those rows are depth 3, and none are deeper (train caps depth at 3) [shown]. That is about 420 refiner parameters per supervised token [computed]. Arm A's loss falls from 2.23 to 0.53 by step 30 and 0.44 by step 40 [shown, result_a.json loss_curve], all inside the 41-step warmup. During those steps W_out = 0, so the gradient into the refiner's 9.4M block and tap parameters is exactly zero (dL/du = W_out^T dL/de = 0) [shown by construction]. Only W_out and the slot vectors learn, as a random-feature readout. When the refiner unblocks, the remaining loss is ~0.13-0.18 nats/token [shown], spread over ~1/10 of the samples per lap count [computed from the 1..8 x1, 9..12 x0.5 weights]. Comparable cases: Project Newt routed <=5% of its signal through the loop and tied a compute-matched one-pass LoRA [shown, single author, unreviewed]. LRT, the positive frozen-refiner case, trained 30 epochs per stage per task [shown, R4]. Coconut with answer-only loss and no curriculum scored 14.4 vs 16.5 for no-CoT [shown]. The likely outcome is STS = P = A within +/-1 [suggested].

F3. Lap 1 can do all the work, and the training puts the work there. Village model. Each of the 2 refiner blocks cross-attends to C, the final-norm states of all ~1.1k-2k context tokens. So at L=1 the refiner is already a 2-hop context reader on top of a full 24-layer backbone pass, and multi-hop does not need a second backbone lap [shown, D6 pseudocode]. The answer loss is applied at a random L in 1..12 with no per-lap target. The objective is therefore minimised by a refiner that writes a good e at lap 1 and makes near-idempotent updates afterwards, so laps 9-12 do no harm [suggested]. Evidence: v1 (the separate from-scratch village model) reached a fixed point within ~3 loops, with state change 6.7 -> 1.8 -> 0.14 [shown]. Closing the Loop saw <=0.01 nats past lap 4 [shown]. Ouro peaks at lap 4 [shown]. Prediction: a flat curve from 2 to 8 within noise. Any rise from 1 to 2 or 4 is confounded: random-L training lowers the lap-1 floor (McLeish train-32: 6.4 GSM8K at test-1 vs 49.4 at test-32 [shown]), and the RMS clamp plus small eta turn the laps into a step-size integrator (e_L ~ e_0 + sum(eta_t) * Delta_1). Such a curve would 'rise with laps' with no new information gained per lap [suggested]. D6 has no control that tells these apart.
serious: S1. Missing control: the same refiner trained at L=1 only (call it R1). P (0 laps) and A32 (LoRA r32) test the pause positions and the parameter count. Neither separates 'an 11.6M context-reading refiner' from 'recurrence'. LRT itself ran this control, a non-recurrent refiner at the same budget: 47.5 vs 56.7 on Countdown [shown]. Without R1, STS@8 > A cannot be credited to the laps.

S2. Validation depth extrapolates past training. Train depth is <= 3 by the data contract. 18.0% of validation rows are depth 4-6 [shown, scheduler.py docstring and counts]. A 'one lap per hop' refiner gets no training signal for hops 4-6. Retrofits extrapolate ~1.5x the supervised depth and then hit a ceiling (Shapiro: 70.3% at depth 18 when supervised to 12, then 10.9% at depth 22) [shown]. On Pdepth (templates seen, deeper stories) arm A loses 8 points, concentrated in Q12 (46.6) and Q4 (56.1) [shown]. Those are exactly the rows that need laps beyond the trained hop count.

S3. The pilot does not test the deployed configuration. In the pilot, STS trains LoRA r16 jointly (22.4M trainable). At LFM scale it is 'frozen, no LoRA' (29.1M refiner only) [shown, D6]. A pilot pass could come from LoRA x slot co-adaptation that will not exist at scale. The frozen-base cap is measured on a nearby model: Qwen3-0.6B with a frozen base scored 22.4-24.0 GSM8K vs 38.5 with a trainable base [shown, Coda-Forno]. D6's F arm (no LoRA) is the one that predicts LFM, and it is listed only as 'diagnostic'.

S4. 'No collapse at 12' is not a stress test here. L=12 is inside the training range (9-12 at weight 0.5), so not collapsing there is guaranteed by construction. The real extrapolation check is 16 or 24 [shown, D6 lap sampling]. Compare Loop-1L B: 40.7 at 8 passes vs 29.6 at 12, just past its 1-8 training range [shown].

S5. Signs of the gate staying shut will be missed. The plan logs eta. The relevant quantity is how far the slots move, ||e_L - e_0|| / rho, together with answer-to-slot attention mass. With the RMS clamp, a small W_out leaves the slots as pause tokens, and STS reduces to P. Pause tokens added only at fine-tuning give 'mixed' gains (Goyal) [shown] and +1.0 on GSM8K in DCA [shown].

S6. Implementation risk that can fail silently. HF 5.20.2 updates Qwen3.5 DeltaNet conv state in place (conv_state.copy_ in the cached path) and replaces recurrent state through update_recurrent_state [shown, read in venv transformers 5.20.2]. A lap fork that fails to restore state, or to crop the 16 attention positions, lets lap t attend to lap t-1's slots. That changes the model without any error being raised [suggested]. If the shim is abandoned for full [context + slots] re-runs, the cost becomes (L+1) x 2k-token passes, about 9-13x arm A's compute, and 418 steps no longer fits the budget [computed].

S7. Village model and LFM are separate here. Mac time-to-first-token (TTFT) is underestimated by about 2x [suggested]. Effective decode bandwidth is 2.45B active x ~4.5 bits ~ 1.38 GB/token x 54.5 tok/s ~ 75 GB/s [computed from the measured 54.5 tok/s], not the 170 GB/s D6 assumes. One 16-slot lap reads ~8.9 GB, which is ~118 ms. L=8 (9 passes) is ~1.05 s for 1 agent and ~1.5 s for 2, not 0.45-0.7 s. This does not decide the pilot, but it shrinks the speed margin D6 scored 9/10.

S8. The noise budget leaves no slack. Seed SD on validation is 0.93 (A) and 0.68 (B) [computed from the three seeds]. With 3 seeds, a true effect of exactly +3.0 over B passes the mean-based mark only ~50% of the time. Clearing it at ~90% needs a true effect of about +3.8 [suggested, normal approximation].
fixes: For F1: one change before training. Pre-register per-depth and per-qtype predictions: the gain must appear on depth >= 3 rows and Q4/Q12, and be ~0 on Q7/Q8 and depth <= 1. Add Pdepth (4,367 rows, templates seen) as a co-primary held-out set, so the lap mechanism is scored where it can act. Keep Ben's validation mark unchanged as the gate. If D6 cannot predict at least +8 on Q4+Q12 in advance, do not run it.

For F2: train in two stages so the LoRA cannot take the signal first. Load each seed's trained arm-A adapter and freeze it. Train only the refiner and slots. Initialise W_out small but non-zero (std 1e-3, or LayerScale 1e-2) so the blocks get gradient from step 1. Give the refiner at least 2,000 steps (~32k rows, still under 0.4 epoch), or shrink it to d_r=256 (~3M parameters) to fit 418 steps. The matching control is A continued for the same extra steps with the same frozen-then-refined schedule (A+). Pass mark: STS@8 >= A+ + 3 and B + 3.

For F3: remove the refiner's direct cross-attention to the context C. The refiner may read only the backbone taps at the 16 slot positions. Then every new piece of context information must come through a new backbone lap, and recurrence becomes the only route to multi-hop. Add a per-lap answer loss with weights rising in t, plus a monotonicity term SiLU(loss_t - loss_{t-1}) (LoopUS / Closing the Loop recipe). Optionally add a per-lap auxiliary loss that decodes the oracle Deriv evidence lines (the village oracle already computes them) so that lap t has a target.

For S1/F3 attribution: add arm R1, the same STS trained at fixed L=1 with the same steps and parameters. Add two eval-only controls on every STS checkpoint. (a) repeat-Delta1: reuse lap 1's update for laps 2..L with no new backbone passes. (b) hold-after-k: stop refiner updates after lap k. Pass the 'laps matter' half only if STS@8 - R1 >= 2.0, STS@8 - repeat-Delta1 >= 1.5, and STS@8 - STS@2 >= 1.0 on the same rows. Evaluate at 16 and 24 as the collapse test, since 12 is inside the training range.

For S3: make the frozen F arm (no LoRA) a co-primary pilot arm, compared against frozen + P (pause, frozen). Only the frozen numbers predict LFM. If F - P_frozen < 2, stop the LFM plan whatever the LoRA arms show.

For S6: before any training run, a unit test. With W_out=0, STS logits must equal 'A + 16 pause tokens' to within 1e-3 at every L. Running two laps with the same e must give identical taps. A gradcheck must pass through one fork-and-restore of the DeltaNet state.

For S7 (LFM only): measure one 16-slot lap on the Mac in mlx before choosing L, and budget TTFT at 75 GB/s. Defaults: K=8 slots and L=4, with laps run only on assistant turns that follow a tool result.
attacks.kill_experiment: One seed on Ben's PC: about 2-3.5 h of 5070 Ti time, $0. Village model only. Train D6 exactly as written (seed 0, 418 steps, bsz 16, LoRA r16 + refiner, random L in 1..12). Then, on the same checkpoint and with no further training, evaluate full validation (8,675 rows) at L = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, plus three eval-only controls at L=8. The controls: (i) swap, with slots from another question; (ii) repeat-Delta1, where lap 1's refiner update is reused for laps 2-8 with no new backbone passes; (iii) zero-refiner, which commits the learned e_0 (pause slots only). Report per depth and per qtype. Pre-registered verdict: the attack is right if STS's best lap score is below 68.7 = A's 3-seed mean 66.72 + 2.0. A true effect at the bar (70.12) would land that low on one seed only ~6% of the time, given seed SD ~0.9. It is also right if STS@8 - repeat-Delta1 < 1.0 or STS@8 - STS@2 < 0.5 on paired rows (laps are decoration), or if the depth >= 3 gain over A is under +3. The attack is wrong if STS@8 >= 70.0 with STS@8 - repeat-Delta1 >= 1.5. Either way the result arrives before anything is spent on 3 seeds x 5 arms.

attacks.label: attack:scale:contrarian
fatal: F1. The laps target the wrong failure, so on tau2 they will be decoration. Thinking-OFF scored 23/40, and 9 of its tasks aborted with too_many_errors after repeating a failing call such as 'User not found' 10 times [shown, RESULTS-mac-lfm25.md]. It passed 23 of the 31 tasks that did not abort (74%). If the 9 aborted tasks would pass at that same rate once unstuck, 23 + 9 x 0.74 = 29.7, which is the thinking-ON score of 30 [suggested, arithmetic on shown numbers]. Thinking-ON had 0 aborts: all 40 runs ended with user_stop [shown, think.json]. On its lookup turns it thinks a median of only ~79 tokens (p90 ~380), against a median of 232 on turns where it replies to the user [shown, think.json; tokens estimated as chars/3.68]. Recovering from 'User not found' is a one-step decision that is visible in the last tool result. A 0-lap pause control (P), a thinking-OFF LoRA trained on the teacher's replies, or a decode-time guard can make that decision. STS argues that laps add retrieval depth (user -> order -> item -> policy), but the scoreboard does not show a depth failure. Prediction: on tau2, STS at 8 laps minus STS at 1 lap is about 0, even if STS beats thinking-OFF [suggested].

F2. The scale-up evaluation cannot detect the gain the design predicts (23 -> ~26). One 40-task, 1-trial run has a binomial SE of about 2.7-3.1 tasks at p = 0.6-0.75. The difference between two arms has an SE of about 4 tasks unpaired (somewhat less paired), plus noise from the Haiku user simulator [suggested]. One 40-task pass on the Mac takes ~3.4 h of wall time with 2 agents [shown, think.json timestamps; mean concurrency 1.95]. The full test is 5 lap settings (1/2/4/8/12) plus the P, A and thinking-OFF controls, about 8 settings. At >=4 trials each that is ~8 x 4 x 3.4 h, about 110 h of Mac time [suggested]. So the gate as written can show neither 'beats thinking-OFF' nor 'score rises with laps' on tau2.
serious: S1. The Mac burst cost is underestimated by about 2.7x. I fitted the measured per-step decode times for 1/2/4/8 agents (18.3/28.2/47.4/87.0 ms) against the bytes of weights each step reads, assuming independent top-4 routing. The fit is t = -4.9 ms + 15.7 ms per GB, about 64 GB/s effective, with every residual under 3 ms [suggested fit on shown data]. A 16-slot lap uses ~41 of the 64 experts in each of the 38 MoE layers. At 4.5 bits that is ~8.9 GB, so ~134 ms per lap. L=8 is 9 passes, about 1.2 s per generation; the design claims 0.45 s. The design's 16/420 = 38 ms figure comes from prefill throughput on prompts of 1k+ tokens, where compute is the limit; it does not apply to a 16-token pass, which is limited by reading weights [suggested]. With 2 agents, while one agent bursts, the other advances only about 1 token per ~140 ms. Averaged over time, each agent then decodes at about 28-30 tok/s (design: 32-33), at or below the 30 tok/s rule [suggested]. Steady decode really is unchanged: 16 extra cached positions per generation add ~0.3% decode time at a 9k context. Per-episode latency is fine: 13.8 generations x 1.2 s is about +17 s, against about +115 s for thinking-ON [suggested].

S2. The pilot gate does not test the recipe that will be scaled up. The pilot trains LoRA r16 and the refiner together (22.4M parameters). The LFM recipe trains the refiner only, on a frozen backbone with no LoRA. That is the pilot's arm F, which the design calls 'diagnostic only'. ALAR, the closest evidence the design cites, also trained LoRA r16 on the base model [shown, R2]. Separately, a CPU probe on frozen, untrained Qwen3.5-0.8B: inserting 16 pause tokens raised answer CE by +0.36 nats, and 68% of 34 validation questions got worse [shown, sb1/d2_probe_2shot.log; this was another design's probe with a different slot string]. In the pilot, LoRA can absorb that penalty; at LFM scale only slot_init and the refiner can.

S3. Distilling from the backbone's own thinking-ON traces is the setting where latent distillation is weakest. Over 553 turns in think.json, thinking length has mean 284 tokens, median 122, p90 712 and p99 2,003. The 10% of turns over 700 tokens hold 48% of all thinking tokens. User-facing text turns average 428 tokens, and ~58% of them mention prices, totals or refunds [shown counts; the price/total detection is a crude regex, so suggested]. Squeezing that into 16 slots means 18x compression on average and 44x at p90. In 'Tale of Two Regimes', on the model's own 350-550-token traces, CODI fell to about a quarter of CoT accuracy (12-15 vs 53) [shown, R2]. The data is small: ALAR used 21K successful rollouts [shown]. Here there are 1,792 chats, about 5.8k turns at ~3.2 turns per chat (Loop-1L counted 322 turns in 100 chats) [shown], plus about 54 successful tau2 episodes per pass over the 74 retail tasks outside the eval set [suggested]. Re-answering 5.8k turns with thinking ON on the Mac takes about 26 h [suggested]. The context also does not match. The LFM2.5 chat template removes the <think> content of assistant turns that come before the last user message [shown, chat_template.jinja], so the teacher's replies were written without its earlier thoughts. STS keeps earlier slots in the cache, so the KL and CODI targets were computed in a different context from the student's [suggested].

S4. Training and deployment run different backbones inside a closed loop. Training must use bf16 on an 80 GB A100. In HF 5.20.2 the LFM2-MoE experts are 3D nn.Parameter tensors (~46 GB in bf16), and the bitsandbytes integration only replaces nn.Linear, so a 'frozen 4-bit base' is not available for them [shown, code]. Deployment is mlx 4-bit. The refiner reads hidden states at layers 18 and 30 and the final norm, then writes back into the same backbone on every lap. Quantization error enters each lap, and the refiner never saw it during training [untested].

S5. Implementation. (a) HF: on the multi-token path with record_past=False, update_conv_state copies the new state into the cache in place. Without an explicit snapshot, the first slots of each lap read the previous lap's last 2 slots as their left conv context. The results are silently wrong and no error is raised [shown, code; consequence suggested]. (b) mlx is easier than the design claims for the lap fork. In mlx_lm 0.32.2, lfm2_moe already accepts input_embeddings, the conv cache entry is reassigned rather than modified, so a snapshot is just a saved reference, and KVCache.trim exists [shown]. (c) The server is the hard part. LRUPromptCache is a trie keyed on token IDs, and LFM's conv cache cannot be trimmed, so a stored cache is reused only when the new prompt extends it exactly [shown]. Slots have no token IDs, the OpenAI-format messages that tau2 sends carry no slots, and the refiner's context memory C would have to be cached next to the KV cache. The current stack already seems to re-prefill most of the prompt on every turn. A fit over 553 turns gives generation time = 10.8 s + 22.4 ms per completion token + 3.4 ms per prompt token, about 23 s of a 42 s turn [shown fit; interpretation suggested]. So 'earlier slots stay cached' needs a server-side slot store; otherwise slots are silently dropped whenever the prompt is re-prefilled.

S6. RL via JOLT+ with a Sonnet judge. (a) rlaif/ is a fake world of files, email and calendar for Qwen3-1.7B, not tau2 retail [shown, SPEC.md]. (b) Cost: Sonnet 5.5 costs $2 / $10 per million input/output tokens [shown]. Transcripts run ~9-10k tokens (final prompt mean 9,037) [shown], so each grade costs about $0.01-0.025. JOLT+ grades both a student group and a teacher group: with G=8 and 16 tasks per step that is 256 grades, about $3-6 per step, and 50 steps cost about $150-300. That is against a few dollars of credit, and Loop-1L's $3 cap already forced cuts to 56 steps [shown]. (c) Rollouts need a custom HF generator for STS (no vLLM), so each step takes GPU hours [suggested]. (d) Collapse: there are only 74 training tasks, and 40% of the reward is the judge's grade. Latent RL collapses without a distilled warm start and a KL anchor (Latent-GRPO; INTACT 42.9 vs 78.8) [shown, R2]. With a reverse-KL anchor plus noise on the update, shrinking the per-lap step size toward 0 is the cheapest way to cut variance, and that switches the laps off [untested].

S7. The pilot budget and controls are weak (the judges' point, which I checked). The run sees 418 x 16 = 6,688 rows, 7.8% of one pass over the 86k rows. At ~4.1 answer tokens per row (EOS included) that is about 27.7k supervised tokens; 1,403 of those rows are depth 3, and training has no depth >=4 while 18% of validation does [shown, counted on a sample of train and on all of validation]. LRT trained 30 epochs per task [shown], and Newt concluded 'budget, not architecture' [shown, unreviewed]. There is no arm with the same refiner trained only at L=1. Training on random lap counts degrades the lap-1 floor (McLeish), so lap 8 minus lap 1 overstates what recurrence adds. The refiner can also cross-attend to the context directly and do all its work in lap 1. With W_out zero-initialised, every refiner weight except W_out and slot_init gets exactly zero gradient at step 0 (dL/du = W_out^T dL/de = 0, and dL/d(eta) = 0) [shown, math]. Adam unblocks this within a few steps, but recurrence starts from nothing.

S8. MoE cost and slot capacity move together. If the slots stay diverse, each lap reads ~64% of all expert weights. If they collapse to near-constant vectors (SoftCoT/EBM-CoT in the LRT paper [shown]), laps get cheap but carry nothing. The v1 village model (a separate, from-scratch model, used only as a prior) reached a fixed point within ~3 loops [shown]. If the same happens here, laps 4-8 cost ~0.7 s per generation for no gain [suggested]. LOOM's expert collapse does not directly apply, because no layer processes its own output. But the backbone -> refiner -> backbone path is still a recurrence on a 16 x 2048 state, held in check only by an RMS clamp [suggested].
fixes: For F1: before building anything for tau2, run the free paired analysis and the repetition-guard baseline (see the kill experiment), and measure the tau2 goal as the gap above thinking-OFF plus the guard. LFM arms: thinking-OFF+guard, P (16 slots, 0 laps), a thinking-OFF LoRA SFT on the teacher's replies, STS trained at L=1 only, and full STS. Pass mark fixed in advance: STS@8 >= max(P, LoRA, STS-L1) + 3 points on the per-turn metric. Proved wrong if STS@8 - STS@1 < 1 point.

For F2: measure the lap curve on a per-turn offline metric, not on episodes. Use M_tool on >=1,500 held-out turns (teacher thinking-ON rollouts on the 74 retail tasks outside the eval set, plus held-out chats), paired across lap counts; the SE is about 1-1.5 points. Use tau2 only for the final A-vs-STS check, with >=4 trials, pass^k, and pairing by task.

For S1: use K=8 slots (~86 ms per lap) or L=4 laps (5 passes: 0.43 s at K=8, 0.67 s at K=16). Pass mark: burst <= 0.7 s and >= 30 tok/s per agent averaged over time in a 2-agent tau2 replay. Time a real 16-token pass on the Mac before training anything.

For S2 and S7: make arm F (no LoRA, the actual scale-up recipe) a primary pilot arm. Add an arm with the same refiner trained at L=1 only, and a parameter-matched LoRA r32 arm (A32). Give every arm the same larger step budget (>=3x), or report score against budget for all arms.

For S3: run silent slots only on tool-call turns (lookup and change turns, median 79-103 thinking tokens). On long user-facing turns keep text thinking or thinking-OFF (a hybrid, as ALAR and Switch did). Use ALAR's action-token cross-entropy as the main loss. For traces over 350 tokens, use KaVa-style per-layer KV targets instead of CODI's single hidden state. Strip slots across user turns so the context matches the chat template.

For S4: train against the mlx 4-bit weights dequantized to bf16 in torch, so the trained function is the deployed one. Check the L=8 minus L=1 gap on 100 turns under both bf16 and dequantized 4-bit; if the 4-bit gap is smaller, the loop is amplifying quantization error.

For S5: in HF, use record_past=True and add a smoke test asserting that the conv and KV state before every lap equals the snapshot taken after the context. In mlx, give slot positions reserved placeholder token IDs plus a per-conversation table of their embeddings, so the token-keyed prompt cache keeps working. Or drop the cross-turn carry of slots entirely, which is safe under re-prefill.

For S6: drop RL with a Sonnet judge from v2. If RL is tried at all, use tau2's own database-check reward (no judge cost), with JOLT+ reverse-KL distillation from the hint-conditioned teacher, a hard spending ledger, the per-lap step size logged with a floor, and a stop rule if the lap curve flattens.

For S8: log the number of distinct experts per layer for each lap, the cosine similarity between slots, and the size of the update relative to the slots, every 50 steps. If laps after lap 3 change the slots by less than 10% of lap 1's change, set L=3 and spend the saved budget elsewhere.
attacks.kill_experiment: Free and takes minutes, on the Mac: from the two existing results.json files (lfm25 = thinking ON, lfm25_nothink = thinking OFF), build a paired win/loss table for the 40 tasks. The attack is right if >=5 of the 7 tasks that thinking-ON gains net are among the 9 too_many_errors aborts, and if thinking-ON's turns at the recovery point think <150 tokens. Confirmation (3.4 h on the Mac; Haiku 5.5 user simulator at $0.10/$0.50 per million tokens, well under $1): rerun thinking-OFF with a guard that refuses a repeated identical failing tool call and returns 'this exact call already failed; try a different method'. If that scores >=28/40, the headroom left for laps is <=2 tasks, below the +-3-4-task noise floor, so STS cannot show its value on tau2. attacks.label: attack:scale:board
fatal: F1. Cross-turn persistence and the carry have nowhere to live on the Mac serving path. Mechanism: tau2's agent re-sends history as plain text without reasoning_content [shown: in sb1/think.json each turn's prompt is a median 12 tokens SHORTER than the previous prompt plus completion]. LFM's chat template drops past <think> spans [shown: chat_template.jinja keep_thinking]. mlx-lm 0.32.2 cannot trim LFM's conv cache (ArraysCache inherits is_trimmable()=False) and only checkpoints the cache at the system-prompt boundary [shown: models/cache.py, server.py _tokenize]. So every turn re-prefills. Fit over 553 turns: time per turn = 12.4 s + 22 ms per output token + 3.2 ms per prompt token; at the mean prompt of 6,801 tokens, about 22 s of the 42 s mean turn tracks prompt length [shown data, suggested reading]. Boards are not tokens, so they vanish at every request. 'Old boards stay in the cache' and Z0 += tanh(g)*Z_R(prev) cannot run as written; it needs a session-stateful server that the design neither costs nor specifies.

F2. The scale-up has no test that could credit the laps. (a) The pilot cannot see the hazard the judges named. My CPU probe on frozen Qwen3.5-0.8B (n=40 validation questions, 2-shot, zero LoRA, which is D2 at init; script sb1/d2_init_probe.py) found D2's laps never hurt [shown, this setup]: answer CE minus pause-slot CE was -0.04 nats at R1, -0.15 at R4, -0.28 at R8 and -0.31 at R12 (SE 0.07); rms(h12)/rms(h8)=1.10, so the norm hold barely bites. On LFM the same band operation took start loss from 0.72 to 2.56 and collapsed at 12 passes [shown, Loop-1L]. So a pilot PASS says nothing about LFM's MoE band. (b) The LFM stage has no pass marks, seeds or controls. The likeliest source of gain is the 9 too_many_errors aborts [shown], and SFT or distillation without any board could fix those. With no 'A + same distillation' arm, any gain is unattributable. (c) 40 tasks x 1 trial has an SD of about 7 points [suggested, repo RESULTS.md]. A gain of 3-4 tasks is invisible.
serious: S1. The distillation data is about 5x smaller than claimed [shown inputs, my arithmetic]. The thinking-ON run did 40 episodes in 3.40 h wall at 2 agents (11.8 episodes/h) with 5,127 completion tokens each, so about 60k tokens/h and about 0.78M in 13 h, not 4M. Four agents add at most 19% aggregate decode (84.6 vs 70.8 tok/s bench), and prefill dominates the turn. 13 h gives about 150-180 episodes, about 110-130 successful (72.5%), about 1.5-1.8k assistant turns. Only tasks 40-113 (74) are clean, since 0-39 are the eval [shown]. tau2 gives episode-level reward only, so ALAR's 'successful turns' is undefined [shown].

S2. The long traces are the hard case and the board is 18-44x smaller than them. Thinking per turn: mean 284 tokens, median 122, p90 712, max 4,361 [shown, chars/3.68]. The 10% of turns over 700 tokens hold 48% of all thinking, with about 22 prices and 24 order/item IDs each, against 1.6 and 2.8 in short turns [shown]. That is the bookkeeping regime where CODI-style single-state targets fell to about 25% of CoT on the model's own 350-550-token traces [shown in Tale of Two Regimes, 1-1.5B math; untested on agents]. KaVa had to zero the CODI loss for stability [shown].

S3. The 'score rises with laps' pass mark can be met with no training [shown, pilot probe]. At init, D2's R-curve already rises monotonically to R12 and recovers 87% of the +0.355 nats that pause slots cost against no slots. The gain is concentrated on SHALLOW questions (R8-R1: -0.36 nats at depth<3 vs -0.09 at depth>=3), the opposite of D2's depth prediction. The per-lap change stays at about 0.12 of |Z0| from lap 4 to lap 12 and never converges, so the planned 'fixed point by lap 3' decoration test passes untrained. Damping matters: undamped slot re-runs (alpha=1, no norm hold) diverge (change grows 0.29 to 0.43 after lap 4) and the gain shrinks past R8 [suggested, within about 1 SE].

S4. The per-lap router bias (8x64) is a dead parameter if it is added the way LFM adds its own expert_bias [shown, code]. That bias only enters top-k selection; routing weights are gathered from the unbiased sigmoid scores (transformers 5.20.2 modeling_lfm2_moe.py l.184-188; mlx-lm 0.32.2 lfm2_moe.py l.213-221), so it gets zero gradient. Added to logits instead, it can only re-weight experts already chosen. The frozen router therefore re-picks experts on every lap. In trained-to-loop MoEs a revisit reuses nearly all experts [shown, SMELT]; frozen-router behaviour on LFM is [untested].

S5. At LFM, less of the board's influence depends on R than in the pilot [shown, config arithmetic]. LFM has no recurrent state, so D2's readout route 3 does not exist. Short conv (L_cache=3) lets only </think> and the next token read the last 2 slots directly. Of 10 attention layers, 4 (2, 6, 10, 14) see the lap-independent init slots, 2 (18, 22) see final-lap band KV, and 4 (26-38) see Z_R. So 40% of the attention read path ignores the laps.

S6. RL as written is a different system with a budget problem. rlaif is LoRA RL on Qwen3-1.7B in a files/email/calendar sandbox, not LFM2.5 or tau2 [shown, SPEC.md, train.py]. Sonnet costs $2/$10 per M [shown, grader.py], and a tau2 transcript is about 4.3k tokens excluding the system prompt, so about $0.011 per grade. JOLT+ with G=4 over 74 tasks is 592 grades ($6.6) plus $1.2 of user simulation, about $7.7 per pass, API only, against 'a few dollars' this week. Loop-1L's $3 cap already forced 56-step runs [shown]. Backprop through 14 turns x R laps of a bf16 24B MoE needs an 80 GB GPU. A deterministic board gives no latent exploration (Dropout-GRPO, Latent-GRPO collapse) [shown, math]. MoE routing flips between rollout and training engines compound over 8 laps x 8 layers [suggested]. The JOLT+ teacher's board can read the privileged reference solution [suggested].

S7. Deployment drift: training is bf16 on GPU but the Mac runs 4-bit, and D2 iterates a quantized 8-layer MoE band 8-12 times per slot (64-96 MoE applications against 8 normally), where a top-4 flip changes the trajectory [untested]. If boards are replayed during re-prefill, replay vs live mismatch also enters (prefill and decode kernels differ) [untested].

S8. Implementation load is the largest in the panel, and none of it exists yet. The repo has no mlx loop code (only backbone/sleep/sleep1_mlx.py) [shown]. The Mac path needs: a custom mlx model with LoRA masked to slot positions; a burst inside BatchGenerator for 2 concurrent agents; ArraysCache snapshot by copy; a session server (F1). HF needs a BoardCache (copy_ in-place updates confirmed at cache_utils.py l.1112/1133 [shown]) plus per-lap upper-stack forks, i.e. about 14 turns x R forks per chat, on an eager per-expert loop [shown].

S9. Speed is NOT the killer, and I concede it [suggested arithmetic]. Decode: 14 boards x 16 slots x 20 KB = 4.6 MB per token against at least 1.3 GB of weights, under 0.5%. Burst: about 0.15-0.3 s against a measured 42 s turn. Memory: negligible. Two caveats: the 35.4 tok/s rule baseline was measured on a short prompt, and at tau2's ~6.8k context the KV reads alone are about 140 MB per token; by D2's own amortised metric at about 60 reply tokens per turn, R=8 with 2 agents lands near 28-29 tok/s.
fixes: F1: v2.0 drops cross-turn persistence and the carry. The board is computed per turn and not kept, which matches LFM's own strip-old-thinking training. Then the Mac only needs a custom burst at prefill. Test persistence later as one change, with a session-keyed mlx server (or deterministic replay of past boards in re-prefill: n-1 bursts at turn n, about +1 s per turn on average). Pass mark for that test: replayed board cosine >= 0.99 with the live one, and >= +2 tasks over no persistence.

F2: (a) Gate LFM training on the free Mac init probe (kill experiment) and change the readout so that D2 at init exactly equals pause for every R: z_out = z_plain + tanh(gamma)*(z_R - z_plain), gamma=0. (b) Pre-register LFM arms with equal data and steps: A + same distillation (no board), C1 (R=1), and D2 at R=8. (c) Use 3 trials on tasks 0-39 with a paired test, and fix the pass mark in advance: D2 >= 27/40 and >= A-distilled + 3 tasks. Wrong if D2 <= A-distilled.
S1: Budget about 65 h of Mac time for 4M tokens, or cut the target. Roll out only tasks 40-113, at least 4 samples per task at temperature 0.7. Keep whole successful episodes.

S2: Use a hybrid: keep text thinking on long or bookkeeping turns (ALAR-style per-turn switch) and use the board only where thinking is under about 300 tokens (78% of turns, 31% of thinking tokens) [shown]. Drop the L1 hidden-state match at first; use CE on reply and tool-call tokens plus reverse-KL.

S3: Report the untrained R-curve as a baseline and require the trained R8-R1 gain to exceed it by >= 2 points. Require the depth signature: gain at depth>=3 > gain at depth<3. Add C1 evaluated at R=8. Replace the change-per-lap test with the swap test.

S4: Delete the router bias. If lap identity is needed, use a lap embedding added to slot inputs or a lap-conditioned LoRA on the router gate weights, so gradient flows through the gathered weights. Log lap-1 vs lap-r expert Jaccard.
S5: Put R-dependence where the answer reads: run the final Z through [0,a) as well, or re-insert Z_R as the slot KV in the lower attention layers. Or choose a band that ends at or after layer 26.

S6: Defer RL. When it comes, port rlaif to tau2 tasks 40-113 with the DB check as the reward and no Sonnet (about $1.2 per pass). Add one-sided noise or a shared dropout mask on the board for exploration. Use routing replay between rollout and training. Keep the KL anchor.
S7: Measure the per-lap board divergence on the Mac (4-bit vs 8-bit, or vs fp16 for the band only) before training. Cap R at the lap where cosine falls below 0.98.
S8: Build the mlx inference path first and smoke-test it against HF on a tiny random lfm2_moe (as loop1l.py --smoke does) before any GPU spend.
S9: State the speed rule at tau2 context length and measure the baseline at 7k tokens.
